AgriKA-GIS: A Spatial-Temporal Framework for High-Resolution Rice Productivity Mapping and Yield Forecasting in Laguna

Argana · Ilagan · Madolora · Praferosa  |  Adviser: Jonalyn G. Ebron  |  Full Thesis Reading Copy (Chapters 1–5)

CHAPTER 1

Introduction

Rice is one of the most important agricultural commodities in the Philippines, serving as both the country's primary staple food and a major source of livelihood for millions of farmers. Ensuring sustainable rice production remains a national priority, with provinces such as Laguna continuing to contribute significantly despite increasing urbanization. Previous studies have demonstrated the value of remote sensing technologies for estimating rice area and yield, supporting more efficient agricultural monitoring and agricultural decision-making (Montecillo, 2011; Relativo et al., 2020).

Recent advances in satellite remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and machine learning have significantly improved the accuracy and efficiency of rice productivity monitoring. Satellite platforms such as Sentinel, together with national initiatives like the Philippine Rice Information System (PRiSM), have demonstrated the potential of integrating geospatial data and predictive models to support agricultural planning and resource management (Mabalay et al., 2022). Likewise, studies have shown that combining multispectral and radar imagery with deep learning techniques enhances the accuracy and robustness of rice yield prediction by capturing complementary information about crop health and environmental conditions (Ramadhani et al., 2020; Fita et al., 2025).

Despite these developments, most existing studies have focused primarily on improving prediction models or generating crop maps, with comparatively limited attention given to transforming prediction outputs into operational decision-support tools for Local Government Units (LGUs). Although accurate yield predictions are valuable, their practical usefulness is limited when they are not presented in a form that enables agriculturists to identify spatial patterns, monitor productivity at finer geographic scales, and prioritize interventions within their jurisdictions. Consequently, there remains a need for an integrated platform that combines predictive analytics with interactive geographic visualization and information management to support evidence-based agricultural monitoring and planning.

To address this gap, this study develops AgriKA-GIS, a Web-based spatial decision-support system for rice productivity monitoring in Laguna. The system integrates an enhanced CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model as its prediction engine, supplying barangay-level spatial yield forecasts that are visualized through an interactive Web-GIS platform. By combining remote sensing, machine learning, spatial databases, and geospatial visualization within a unified system, AgriKA-GIS transforms rice yield predictions into geographically actionable information that supports monitoring, planning, and decision-making for LGU agriculture offices.

Background of the Study

The province of Laguna remains one of the agriculturally active areas in CALABARZON, with rice farming continuing to support local livelihoods despite rapid urbanization. Laguna contributed 36.9% of the region’s total palay output in 2024, making efficient rice productivity monitoring important for local agricultural planning. At the ground level, City Agriculture Offices and rice technicians serve as the primary link between LGUs and farming communities by monitoring crop conditions, coordinating farmer reports, and preparing seasonal production data.

At present, rice yield monitoring in many LGUs still relies heavily on manual reporting. Farmers usually provide planting and harvest information through phone calls, messaging applications, direct visits, or field consultations. Rice technicians then encode these reports into standardized forms, often using spreadsheets, before submitting them to provincial or regional offices. While this process is already institutionalized, it is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and dependent on the accuracy of farmer self-reporting. Because production data are often consolidated after field conditions have already changed, delayed reporting can limit the ability of agriculture offices to respond promptly to low-yield areas, crop stress, or emerging production problems.

Over the years, Sta Rosa’s historical rice yields have gone through a two-fold decline. Upon analysing the Dry Season (DS) and Wet Season (WS) data from 2021 to 2026, a downward trajectory was observed in both agricultural efficiency (yield) and agricultural capacity (harvested area).

1. Declining Rice Yield (MT/Ha)

Efficiency is dropping. While the yield hovered comfortably around 5.0 to 5.1 MT/Ha in 2021 and early 2022, it has seen a noticeable decline in recent years. By the 2024 Wet Season, yield plummeted to roughly 3.77 MT/Ha, and has only recovered to about 4.48 MT/Ha by early 2026.

2. Shrinking Harvested Area

Even more critically, the total land actually being harvested is shrinking drastically. In the 2021 Dry Season, 161.5 hectares were harvested. By the 2026 Dry Season, this figure dropped to just 51.7 hectares.

Rice production in Cabuyao has become increasingly vulnerable despite maintaining an average yield of approximately 4.5 metric tons per hectare. Over the years, the municipality has experienced a continuous reduction in agricultural land due to rapid urbanization, resulting in fewer areas available for rice cultivation. At the same time, rice production is challenged by climate-related hazards such as drought, flooding, typhoons, and groundwater scarcity, as well as long-term issues including soil degradation and an aging farming population. These factors create uncertainty in future rice production, making it more difficult for the City Agriculture Office to accurately estimate harvest outputs and implement timely agricultural interventions.

Given these challenges, predicting rice yield has become increasingly important for supporting agricultural planning and decision-making. A reliable prediction system can provide advance estimates of rice production, allowing agricultural officials to anticipate potential production shortages, allocate resources more efficiently, prioritize monitoring efforts, and prepare appropriate interventions before harvest. By integrating historical production records with environmental and climatic data, rice yield prediction can help improve the responsiveness and effectiveness of local agricultural management while promoting more sustainable rice production in Cabuyao.

Historical accounts from the Biñan City Agriculture Office indicate that while rice yield per hectare has remained relatively stable at around 3.6–3.7 tons per hectare, the city's overall rice production capacity has steadily declined due to rapid urbanization. Rice farming areas have decreased from more than 600 hectares in the early 2000s to approximately 20 hectares today as agricultural lands have been converted into residential and industrial developments. Additionally, prolonged droughts, increasing labor costs, an aging farming population, and the continuous decline in active rice farmers have made rice production increasingly uncertain.

These conditions highlight the importance of rice yield prediction. Even when yield per hectare remains relatively stable, the combined effects of shrinking agricultural land, climate variability, and socioeconomic challenges make future rice production difficult to anticipate. Predictive models can therefore support local government units by providing advance estimates of rice yield, enabling timely interventions, more efficient resource allocation, and improved agricultural planning.

Based on the interview with the Calamba City Agriculture Office, no clear long-term trend of increasing or declining rice yield was identified. Instead, the interview revealed that rice production monitoring remains largely manual, relying on field inspections, pest monitoring, and harvest reports submitted by farmers. While these methods provide records of harvested areas and production, they offer limited capability for analyzing historical yield patterns or forecasting future rice production.

These limitations highlight the need for rice yield prediction. By integrating historical production records with weather, soil, and satellite-derived information, predictive models can provide advanced estimates of rice yield, enabling the City Agriculture Office to identify areas with potentially low production, support timely interventions, and improve agricultural planning and resource allocation beyond traditional manual monitoring.

The previous AgriKA system developed by Ebron et al. (2025) addressed part of this challenge by introducing a CNN-LSTM deep learning model for rice yield prediction using Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, weather data, and historical yield records. The system demonstrated the feasibility of using satellite-based and machine learning-driven methods for rice yield forecasting in Laguna. It also provided a web-based map interface that allowed users to view predicted yields and compare seasonal production trends. Their final model was able to yield the following model metrics.

However, the previous AgriKA system remained limited in spatial granularity. Its map output represented each city or municipality as a single aggregated yield value, which prevented users from identifying productivity differences among barangays. This limitation reduces the practical usefulness of the system for City Agriculturists and Rice Technicians, who often need to know which specific barangays are underperforming, where field validation should be prioritized, and where agricultural interventions may be needed. Since rice productivity can vary within the same municipality due to differences in irrigation access, soil conditions, planting schedules, and localized environmental factors, barangay-level visualization is necessary for more location-specific agricultural decision-making.

In addition, the previous AgriKA model primarily relied on Sentinel-2 optical imagery, which can be affected by cloud cover in tropical environments such as the Philippines. Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) provides complementary information because it can capture surface and crop-related conditions regardless of cloud cover or lighting conditions. Integrating Sentinel-1 SAR-derived information with Sentinel-2 vegetation indices, meteorological data, and historical yield records may therefore improve the robustness of rice yield prediction.

In response to these limitations, this study proposes AgriKA-GIS, a Web-based spatial decision-support system that extends the previous AgriKA model through enhanced rice yield prediction, barangay-level visualization, residual error mapping, and role-based data management. By transforming prediction outputs into interactive geographic visualizations, AgriKA-GIS aims to help LGU agriculture offices monitor rice productivity more effectively, identify spatial patterns of yield variation, and support evidence-based planning and intervention at the barangay level. This study seeks to bridge the gap between advanced rice yield prediction models and their practical application in local agricultural management. By integrating enhanced predictive analytics with interactive geospatial visualization and secure information management, AgriKA-GIS aims to provide LGU agriculture offices with a more comprehensive, accurate, and spatially informed decision-support platform that strengthens evidence-based monitoring, planning, and resource allocation for rice production in Laguna.

Statement of the Problem

Rice yield monitoring in the province of Laguna currently depends on manual reporting practices. Farmers relay harvest information verbally through phone calls or messaging applications, and rice technicians encode this data into standardized Excel forms that are submitted bi-monthly to the provincial office. Although these methods are institutionalized, they are slow, labor-intensive, and dependent on the accuracy of farmer self-reporting, contributing to delays in intervention and inconsistencies in reported yield figures (Rotairo et al., 2019; Mosleh et al., 2015). Without a consolidated geographic view of rice productivity, city agriculturists cannot readily identify which specific areas within their jurisdiction are underperforming or determine where to prioritize field visits and agricultural interventions.

The previous AgriKA system (Ebron et al., 2025) addressed part of this challenge by introducing a CNN-LSTM deep learning model that predicts rice yield using Sentinel-2 satellite imagery and meteorological data. However, its spatial output was limited to the municipality level, where each city was represented by a single aggregated yield value. As a result, variations in rice productivity among barangays remain invisible to its users. City agriculturists are unable to distinguish which barangays are performing better or worse than others, nor can they identify where the model consistently over-predicts or under-predicts yield. This limitation is significant because studies have shown that rice yield varies considerably within municipal boundaries due to differences in irrigation availability, soil conditions, planting schedules, and local microclimatic factors (Zhou et al., 2023; Jeong et al., 2021). Consequently, municipality-level aggregation limits the usefulness of prediction results for location-specific agricultural planning and resource allocation.

Apart from its limited spatial granularity, the previous AgriKA system primarily relied on Sentinel-2 optical imagery. While Sentinel-2 provides valuable vegetation information through indices such as NDVI, EVI, and NDWI, its effectiveness can be constrained by persistent cloud cover, particularly in tropical countries such as the Philippines. Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), on the other hand, provides complementary observations by penetrating cloud cover and capturing information related to soil moisture and crop conditions regardless of weather or time of day. Incorporating Sentinel-1 alongside Sentinel-2 therefore presents an opportunity to improve the robustness and reliability of rice yield prediction.

Furthermore, the previous AgriKA system does not provide mechanisms for barangay-level agricultural data management, spatial error visualization, or role-based access control that reflects the operational workflow of Local Government Unit (LGU) agriculture offices. These limitations reduce the system's effectiveness as a practical decision-support tool for city agriculturists and rice technicians responsible for monitoring rice production and implementing location-specific agricultural interventions.

Given these limitations, this study seeks to determine whether integrating Sentinel-1 SAR-derived information into the existing CNN-LSTM model, implementing barangay-level spatial analysis through a Web-GIS platform, and incorporating spatial error visualization and role-based data management can significantly improve rice yield prediction performance and enhance spatial decision support for Local Government Unit agriculture offices in Laguna. Specifically, the study aims to determine whether these enhancements provide more accurate yield predictions, better geographic representation of rice productivity, and greater usability for agricultural monitoring and decision-making compared with the previous AgriKA system.

Objectives of the Study

General Objective

To determine whether extending the existing AgriKA CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model through the integration of Sentinel-1 SAR-derived information, barangay-level spatial analysis, and a Web-GIS platform improves rice yield prediction performance and spatial decision support for Local Government Unit (LGU) agriculture offices in Laguna.

Specific Objectives:

1. To develop and evaluate an extended CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model by integrating Sentinel-1 SAR-derived information with Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, meteorological variables, and historical rice yield data for barangay-level rice yield prediction in Laguna.

To accomplish this objective, the study will extend the existing AgriKA CNN-LSTM architecture by incorporating Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)-derived information alongside Sentinel-2 multispectral vegetation indices, meteorological variables, and historical rice yield records. The integration of complementary radar and optical remote sensing information will be investigated to determine its contribution to barangay-level rice yield prediction while reducing the limitations associated with cloud cover in optical imagery. The resulting prediction model will serve as the prediction engine of the proposed system. The predictive performance of the enhanced model will be evaluated using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the Coefficient of Determination (R²), and compared with the previous AgriKA model to determine whether the integration of Sentinel-1 information provides measurable improvements in prediction performance.

2. To develop and evaluate a Web-based spatial decision-support system for barangay-level rice productivity monitoring in Laguna that enables visualization of predicted rice yields, residual maps, and spatial productivity trends to support agricultural monitoring and evidence-based decision-making by Local Government Unit (LGU) agriculture offices.

To accomplish this objective, the study will develop a Web-based spatial decision-support system that integrates rice yield prediction with Geographic Information System (GIS) technologies to provide interactive barangay-level visualization of predicted rice yields and agricultural information. The system will enable authorized users to visualize rice productivity through thematic maps, monitor productivity trends across cropping seasons, and organize agricultural information within a centralized platform. In addition, the system will generate barangay-level residual maps by calculating the differences between predicted and observed rice yields. These maps will visually represent prediction errors, allowing users to identify areas where the model overestimates or underestimates rice productivity, recognize locations requiring field validation, and better interpret the reliability of prediction results across different barangays.The developed Web-based spatial decision-support system will be evaluated through User Acceptance Testing (UAT) using a structured questionnaire based on the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Quality Model.

3. To develop and evaluate a secure automated data pipeline for acquiring, processing, integrating, and managing Sentinel-1 SAR imagery, Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, meteorological variables, and historical rice yield data to support barangay-level rice yield prediction and spatial visualization.

To accomplish this objective, the study will develop a secure data pipeline that automates the collection, preprocessing, storage, and integration of Sentinel-1 SAR imagery, Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, meteorological data, and historical rice yield records into a centralized spatial database. The pipeline will support consistent preparation of multi-source datasets required by the extended CNN-LSTM prediction model and the Web-based spatial decision-support system. The developed pipeline will facilitate efficient updating of remote sensing datasets while maintaining data integrity, consistency, and secure management throughout the prediction workflow. The pipeline will be evaluated based on its ability to reliably acquire, preprocess, integrate, and deliver data required for rice yield prediction and spatial visualization.

Rationale of the Study

The push toward more data-driven and technology-enabled approaches to agricultural management in the Philippines has gained significant momentum in recent years. Under the Department of Agriculture's Agriculture 4.0 agenda, there is a clear national direction toward integrating precision agriculture tools including satellite monitoring, AI-based prediction, and digital farm management systems, into local agricultural practice (Cordero & Park, 2023). In reality, however, these tools have not yet reached the LGU level in a form that city agriculture offices can realistically adopt and use on a day-to-day basis. AgriKA-GIS addresses this gap directly by taking a validated deep learning model that has already demonstrated feasibility in the local context and making its outputs more spatially meaningful and more accessible to the practitioners on the ground.

For city agriculturists and rice technicians in Cabuyao, Calamba, Biñan, and Santa Rosa, the most immediate benefit of AgriKA-GIS is a clearer, more location-specific view of rice yield conditions across their jurisdiction. Rather than working from aggregated municipal summaries compiled through manual reporting, these officers would be able to see which barangays within their city are showing lower predicted yields relative to others, and respond accordingly. Research has consistently found that presenting agricultural AI outputs through interactive spatial maps, rather than tables or charts, increases how much government users trust and act on that information, particularly among officers who are not formally trained in data analysis (Panda et al., 2025; Odion et al., 2023). Making the information both spatial and accessible, in other words, is not just a design preference. It is what determines whether the system gets used in practice.

Beyond its immediate operational benefits, this study is aligned with several Sustainable Development Goals that reflect its broader relevance to Philippine society. Its primary alignment is with SDG 2 (Zero Hunger, Target 2.4), which calls for sustainable food production systems and resilient agricultural practices. By enabling more informed, location-specific monitoring of rice yield conditions, AgriKA-GIS supports the ability of LGU officers to identify underperforming areas earlier and coordinate interventions before losses compound, a contribution to the long-term sustainability of rice production in urbanizing municipalities where agricultural land and labor are already declining. The use of open-source satellite data and a deployable web architecture contributes to SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure, Target 9.4) by bringing accessible geospatial technology tools to local agricultural infrastructure without requiring expensive proprietary systems. Its support for more informed land use monitoring at the barangay level connects to SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities, Target 11.3), particularly in cities like Biñan and Santa Rosa where the boundary between agricultural and industrial land is actively shifting. Finally, the system's capacity to surface yield changes tied to seasonal weather variation contributes to SDG 13 (Climate Action, Target 13.1) by giving LGU officers a spatial basis for understanding how climate-related factors are affecting productivity across different parts of their jurisdiction.

The system does not claim to fully resolve any of these challenges. It is a decision-support tool, and its value depends on the quality of data available to it and the willingness of its users to engage with it. What it does offer is a more spatially grounded foundation for agricultural monitoring at the LGU level, one that builds on an already validated model rather than starting from scratch, and that is designed around the actual workflows and institutional structures of the offices it is meant to serve. Ultimately, this study seeks to bridge the gap between advances in remote sensing, artificial intelligence, and geospatial technologies and their practical application within Local Government Units by providing a localized, spatially enabled decision-support system that supports more informed, timely, and evidence-based agricultural monitoring and planning.

Scope and Delimitations of the Study

This study focuses on the development and evaluation of AgriKA-GIS, a Web-based spatial decision-support system for barangay-level rice productivity monitoring in Laguna. The system is intended to support City Agriculturists, Rice Technicians, and other authorized LGU personnel by providing spatially organized rice yield information for agricultural monitoring and planning.

Specifically, the study:

- develops a Web-based Geographic Information System (Web-GIS) that visualizes predicted rice productivity at the barangay level;

- integrates rice yield prediction with interactive spatial visualization to support agricultural monitoring and decision-making;

- provides spatial decision-support features, including barangay-level rice yield heatmaps, residual maps, seasonal visualization, and municipality-based filtering;

- includes a role-based data management system that enables secure, municipality-specific access to rice yield information for authorized users;

- evaluates the predictive performance of the enhanced rice yield prediction model using appropriate regression performance metrics; and

- evaluates the usability and acceptability of the developed system using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model.

The geographic scope of the study is limited to the selected cities of Biñan, Cabuyao, Calamba, and Santa Rosa in the Province of Laguna. These cities were selected to maintain consistency with the previous AgriKA study, facilitate direct comparison between the baseline and enhanced systems, and ensure the availability of historical rice yield records, satellite imagery, and stakeholder participation for system evaluation. Laguna also represents an appropriate study area because of its significant contribution to regional rice production and its continuing transition toward increasingly urbanized agricultural landscapes.

Delimitations of the Study

This study is subject to the following delimitations:

- The research focuses exclusively on rice productivity monitoring and yield prediction. Consequently, the developed prediction model and Web-GIS platform are intended only for rice and cannot be directly applied to other agricultural commodities without additional model development and validation.

- The implementation and evaluation of AgriKA-GIS are limited to the selected cities of Biñan, Cabuyao, Calamba, and Santa Rosa in Laguna. Therefore, the findings may not be directly generalizable to other provinces or regions with different agricultural, climatic, and operational conditions.

- The predictive performance of the developed system depends on the availability, completeness, temporal consistency, and quality of historical rice yield records, satellite imagery, and meteorological data used in the study.

- Standardized barangay-level georeferenced soil quality datasets are not incorporated as direct model inputs because they are not consistently available across the participating Local Government Units. Instead, remotely sensed environmental variables are utilized to represent field conditions relevant to rice productivity.

- Rice yield predictions generated by AgriKA-GIS are intended to provide decision-support information and should not be interpreted as exact representations of actual field conditions or official production estimates.

- AgriKA-GIS complements existing agricultural monitoring practices but is not intended to replace official field inspections, crop damage assessments, production surveys, or agricultural reports conducted by the Department of Agriculture, PhilRice, or Local Government Units.

- System operation depends on a stable internet connection to access online geospatial services, satellite-derived datasets, and other web-based resources. Offline functionality is beyond the scope of the study.

- The study is limited to satellite-based monitoring and does not incorporate Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), automated irrigation management, or other advanced precision agriculture technologies.

- The Web-GIS platform focuses on barangay-level rice yield visualization, residual mapping, seasonal comparison, and municipality-based filtering. Advanced spatial analyses, such as hotspot analysis, spatial autocorrelation, geostatistical interpolation, and predictive spatial simulation, are beyond the scope of this research.

- The developed system is evaluated using available historical datasets and user acceptance testing. Long-term operational deployment, continuous system monitoring, and assessment of long-term impacts on agricultural productivity are not included within the scope of this study.

Conceptual Framework

The conceptual framework of AgriKA-GIS is structured around a six-component pipeline, Input, Preprocessing, CNN-LSTM, GIS Integration, Evaluation, and Output, that illustrates how remote sensing data, ground-based agricultural records, and geospatial technologies are combined to produce a spatially actionable rice yield monitoring platform for Local Government Unit (LGU) use. This structure extends the conventional Input-Process-Output (IPO) model by expanding the traditional "Process" stage into four distinct phases: Preprocessing, CNN-LSTM Prediction, GIS Integration, and Evaluation. Together with the Input and Output components, these form the six components of the framework. Each represents a conceptually and technically different operation, allowing the framework to clearly illustrate the transformation of raw agricultural and geospatial data into a Web-based spatial decision-support system.

Figure 1. Proposed Conceptual Framework

The conceptual framework of the proposed study illustrates how the researchers intend to integrate remote sensing, machine learning, and GIS technologies to develop a Web-based decision-support system for barangay-level rice yield monitoring in Laguna. The framework serves as the blueprint of the study by presenting the logical flow of data from collection, processing, prediction, visualization, evaluation, and ultimately to the generation of spatial information that supports agricultural monitoring and decision-making. Through this framework, the researchers demonstrate how various datasets and technologies are combined to address the limitations of the existing AgriKA system, particularly its municipality-level visualization and the absence of a mechanism for displaying prediction errors at the barangay level.

Unlike the previous AgriKA system, which presents rice yield predictions only at the municipal level, the proposed AgriKA-GIS extends the existing framework by integrating GIS technologies to visualize predicted rice yields at the barangay level. The researchers believe that presenting prediction results through interactive spatial visualization allows City Agriculturists and Rice Technicians to better understand the geographic distribution of rice productivity and identify locations that may require field validation or agricultural intervention. The framework is therefore organized into six major components, Input, Preprocessing, CNN-LSTM, GIS Integration, Evaluation, and Output, representing the sequential activities undertaken throughout the study.

Input

The first component of the framework consists of the datasets required for developing the enhanced rice yield prediction model and the Web-GIS platform. The researchers gather historical rice yield records from PhilRice and participating City Agriculture Offices to serve as the reference or ground-truth data for model training and validation. These historical records provide information regarding previous rice production and establish the baseline against which the prediction model is evaluated.

To represent crop conditions, the researchers utilize multispectral satellite imagery obtained from Sentinel-2. From these satellite images, vegetation indices such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), and Green Ratio are extracted because these indicators have been widely used in previous studies to describe vegetation health and crop vigor. Recognizing that optical satellite imagery is often affected by cloud cover, particularly in tropical regions such as the Philippines, the researchers also incorporate Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery. Sentinel-1 provides soil moisture indicators that complement the vegetation indices by capturing information related to ground conditions regardless of weather conditions. This integration of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 is expected to provide more comprehensive environmental information for rice yield prediction.

In addition to satellite-derived information, the researchers collect meteorological variables, including rainfall, temperature, and humidity, from the Open-Meteo API. These environmental variables are incorporated because rice productivity is strongly influenced by weather conditions throughout the cropping season. Finally, barangay boundary shapefiles are obtained to provide the geographic boundaries required for spatial visualization within the Web-GIS platform. Rather than functioning as predictive variables, these spatial datasets enable the visualization of predicted rice yields according to the administrative boundaries used by the participating Local Government Units.

Preprocessing

After collecting the required datasets, the researchers preprocess the data to ensure that they are suitable for machine learning. During this phase, satellite imagery is processed to derive vegetation indices and soil moisture indicators, while meteorological data are cleaned, normalized, and synchronized according to the rice cropping calendar. Historical rice yield records are also examined for completeness and consistency, and missing values are addressed using appropriate imputation techniques to minimize the effects of incomplete data during model training.

CNN-LSTM

Following preprocessing, the prepared datasets are supplied to the enhanced CNN-LSTM model. The researchers retain the CNN-LSTM architecture established by the previous AgriKA study because it has already demonstrated its capability to predict rice yield using remotely sensed and meteorological data. Within the model, the CNN extracts spatial characteristics from the satellite-derived features, while the LSTM network captures temporal relationships among historical rice yield records and weather variables. By incorporating Sentinel-1 soil moisture indicators alongside Sentinel-2 vegetation indices, the researchers aim to improve the robustness of the prediction model by providing additional environmental information that may influence rice productivity. The output of this phase is the predicted rice yield values that will subsequently be visualized within the Web-GIS platform.

GIS Integration

Once the rice yield predictions have been generated, the researchers integrate the prediction results into a Geographic Information System to transform numerical outputs into spatially meaningful information. The predicted rice yields are stored in a PostgreSQL/PostGIS spatial database and linked with the corresponding barangay boundaries. This enables the Web-GIS platform to display the predictions as an interactive barangay-level rice yield heatmap using Leaflet.js.

The researchers also incorporate basic filtering functions that allow users to visualize predictions by city and cropping season. These filters enable City Agriculturists and Rice Technicians to examine rice productivity within specific localities and compare predicted yields across different planting periods. Rather than providing advanced spatial analysis, the system focuses on presenting prediction results through an intuitive and interactive geographic interface that supports routine agricultural monitoring.

To further assist users in interpreting the model's performance, the researchers generate a barangay-level residual map by comparing the recorded rice yield with the corresponding predicted rice yield. Residual values are calculated as the difference between the recorded (observed) and predicted yields and are displayed using graduated colors to indicate areas where the model over-predicts or under-predicts rice productivity. Instead of conducting advanced spatial statistical analysis, the residual map serves as a visual aid that helps users recognize where prediction errors occur and identify locations that may require further validation through field inspection.

Evaluation

The researchers evaluate the proposed system from two perspectives: predictive performance and software quality. The predictive capability of the enhanced CNN-LSTM model is assessed using standard regression metrics, including Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the coefficient of determination (R²). These evaluation metrics determine the extent to which the predicted rice yields correspond to the recorded yield data and allow comparison between the enhanced model and the existing AgriKA model.

The developed Web-GIS platform is likewise evaluated through UAT using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model. The evaluation focuses on the quality characteristics most relevant to the proposed system, namely functional suitability, usability, performance efficiency, and reliability. City Agriculturists and Rice Technicians from the participating Local Government Units will serve as respondents to determine whether the system effectively supports their agricultural monitoring activities and whether the Web-GIS interface is practical and easy to use in their operational environment.

Output

The final output of the study is a Web-GIS-based decision-support platform that combines rice yield prediction with interactive spatial visualization. Specifically, the system provides an interactive barangay-level rice yield heatmap that enables users to visualize predicted rice productivity across the selected rice-producing barangays of Calamba, Cabuyao, Santa Rosa, and Biñan. It also presents a barangay-level residual map that highlights areas where the prediction model over-predicts or under-predicts rice yield relative to the available recorded data. The platform further includes a role-based dashboard that allows authorized users to access prediction results through basic filtering by city and cropping season.

Through these outputs, the researchers envision AgriKA-GIS as a practical decision-support tool that complements existing agricultural monitoring practices. Rather than replacing field inspections or official production reports, the system is intended to provide City Agriculture Offices with a spatial representation of predicted rice productivity that supports more informed planning, monitoring, and resource allocation. By integrating machine learning and Web-GIS technologies, the proposed study seeks to transform rice yield prediction into geographically meaningful information that is more accessible and useful for local agricultural decision-makers.

CHAPTER 2

Review of Related Literature

Review of Literature

2.1 Rice Production and Agricultural Monitoring in the Philippines

Rice remains the cornerstone of Philippine agriculture, serving not only as the country's primary staple food but also as a major source of income for millions of Filipino farmers. Beyond ensuring food security, the rice sector contributes significantly to rural employment, local economic development, and national agricultural productivity (Seck et al., 2012; Casinillo et al., 2023). According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (2024), Laguna accounted for approximately 36.9% of the total palay production in the CALABARZON Region in 2024, making it one of the region's leading rice-producing provinces despite experiencing rapid urbanization and industrial expansion. At the national level, approximately 4.72 million hectares of agricultural land are devoted to rice cultivation, producing nearly 19 million metric tons annually (Samoy-Pascual et al., 2022). These figures emphasize the continued importance of rice production to the country's economy and food supply while underscoring the need for efficient monitoring systems capable of supporting sustainable agricultural management.

Rice productivity is influenced by a combination of environmental, climatic, and management factors that vary throughout the cropping season. Temperature, rainfall, irrigation availability, and seasonal weather patterns directly affect crop growth and ultimately determine yield performance (Gutierrez et al., 2019; Li et al., 2025). Recent studies have further shown that climate change has intensified production risks through prolonged droughts, irregular rainfall patterns, flooding, and increasing temperatures, all of which contribute to declining rice productivity and threaten long-term food security (Li et al., 2025; Samoy-Pascual et al., 2022). These findings highlight the importance of continuously monitoring crop conditions throughout the growing season to support timely agricultural interventions and adaptive management strategies.

Despite the strategic importance of rice production, agricultural monitoring practices in many developing countries, including the Philippines, remain largely dependent on conventional data collection methods. Agricultural production information is commonly gathered through field inspections, farmer interviews, and self-reported harvest records before being manually consolidated into spreadsheets and periodic reports (Mosleh et al., 2015). Within Philippine Local Government Units (LGUs), rice technicians and city agriculturists typically collect production data through field visits, telephone calls, messaging applications, and interviews with farmers before submitting reports to provincial and regional offices. While these procedures remain institutionalized, they are often labor-intensive, time-consuming, and susceptible to reporting delays and inaccuracies associated with self-reported production data (Lagrazon & Tan, 2023; Parreño & Anter, 2024). As a result, agricultural officers frequently receive production information only after significant delays, reducing their ability to respond promptly to emerging production issues or allocate resources efficiently.

Another challenge identified in the literature is the limited spatial detail provided by existing agricultural monitoring systems. Official production statistics are generally reported at municipal, provincial, or regional levels, providing an overview of agricultural performance but offering little information about productivity differences among smaller administrative units such as barangays. However, agricultural productivity is inherently spatially heterogeneous because variations in soil characteristics, irrigation availability, cropping schedules, and local environmental conditions can produce significantly different yield outcomes even within the same municipality (Gutierrez et al., 2019; Li et al., 2025). Consequently, aggregated production reports often provide insufficient geographic information for location-specific planning, monitoring, and intervention at the Local Government Unit level.

In response to these challenges, recent developments in digital agriculture have introduced technologies that improve the efficiency and accuracy of agricultural monitoring. The integration of remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), artificial intelligence, and web-based information systems enables continuous observation of crop conditions, automated processing of agricultural data, and timely dissemination of spatial information for decision-makers. National initiatives such as the Philippine Rice Information System (PRiSM) demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating satellite imagery with predictive technologies to support large-scale rice monitoring and production assessment (Mabalay et al., 2022). Similarly, the Department of Agriculture's Agriculture 4.0 initiative promotes the adoption of digital technologies to modernize agricultural management and improve evidence-based decision-making throughout the country (Cordero & Park, 2023). Nevertheless, these technological innovations remain primarily focused on national or regional agricultural monitoring, with relatively limited implementation in operational decision-support systems tailored to the routine workflows and information requirements of Local Government Unit agriculture offices.

Synthesis

The reviewed literature consistently establishes that rice production remains fundamental to Philippine food security and economic development, while also demonstrating that rice productivity is increasingly affected by environmental variability and climate-related challenges (Li et al., 2025; Samoy-Pascual et al., 2022). Although existing agricultural monitoring systems continue to support government reporting, they remain heavily dependent on manual data collection, periodic reporting, and aggregated production statistics that provide limited spatial information for local decision-making (Mosleh et al., 2015; Lagrazon & Tan, 2023; Parreño & Anter, 2024). Recent advances in digital agriculture, including remote sensing, GIS, and artificial intelligence, have significantly improved agricultural monitoring capabilities at national and regional scales (Mabalay et al., 2022; Cordero & Park, 2023). However, there remains a noticeable gap in translating these technologies into localized, spatially enabled decision-support systems that address the operational needs of Local Government Units. This gap provides the rationale for the present study, which proposes AgriKA-GIS as a Web-based Geographic Information System that integrates predictive analytics and interactive spatial visualization to support barangay-level rice productivity monitoring and evidence-based agricultural decision-making in Laguna.

2.2 Remote Sensing for Rice Monitoring

Remote sensing has become one of the most significant technological advancements in modern agriculture because it enables continuous, large-scale, and non-destructive monitoring of crop conditions without relying solely on labor-intensive field inspections. Through satellite observations, researchers and agricultural agencies can monitor vegetation growth, crop health, planting schedules, soil moisture, and environmental conditions over extensive agricultural landscapes in a timely and cost-effective manner (Mosleh et al., 2015). Compared with traditional field-based monitoring, remote sensing provides wider spatial coverage, more frequent observations, and objective measurements that support precision agriculture, crop forecasting, and evidence-based agricultural management. These advantages have made remote sensing an essential component of modern agricultural monitoring systems, particularly in regions where timely field data collection is constrained by limited manpower and extensive agricultural areas.

Among the satellite platforms currently available for agricultural applications, the Sentinel missions developed under the European Space Agency's Copernicus Programme have become some of the most widely adopted because of their free accessibility, frequent revisit intervals, and high spatial resolution (Fernandez-Beltran et al., 2021). Sentinel-2 is particularly valuable for monitoring vegetation because it captures multispectral optical imagery that enables the computation of vegetation indices such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), and Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI). These indices have been extensively used to estimate vegetation vigor, chlorophyll content, biomass, canopy development, and crop health, making them reliable indicators of rice growth and productivity (Fernandez-Beltran et al., 2021; Ebron et al., 2025). Recent studies further suggest that integrating multiple vegetation indices provides a more comprehensive representation of crop conditions than relying on NDVI alone. Fita et al. (2025) observed that the relationship between vegetation indices and rice yield varies across crop growth stages, while Saini and Nagpal (2024) demonstrated that combining multiple spectral features within deep learning models improved prediction accuracy compared with single-index approaches. These findings indicate that multispectral imagery provides valuable information for monitoring crop development throughout the growing season.

Despite the effectiveness of optical imagery, its performance is often limited by persistent cloud cover, a common challenge in tropical countries such as the Philippines. To overcome this limitation, researchers increasingly utilize Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), which actively transmits microwave signals capable of penetrating clouds and acquiring imagery regardless of weather conditions or time of day (Wu et al., 2020). Unlike optical sensors that primarily capture vegetation reflectance, Sentinel-1 provides information related to crop structure, surface roughness, and soil moisture, allowing continuous monitoring even during cloudy periods. Studies conducted under Philippine agricultural conditions have demonstrated the reliability of Sentinel-1 for rice monitoring. Gutierrez et al. (2019) successfully used multi-temporal Sentinel-1 imagery to determine rice planting windows across the Philippines, while Relativo et al. (2020) established significant relationships between SAR backscatter values and rice yield in Laguna. Likewise, Bolanio et al. (2024) reported an overall classification accuracy of 96.5% and approximately 83% confidence in rice yield estimation using Sentinel-1A C-band SAR imagery in Agusan del Sur. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that SAR imagery provides dependable observations for rice monitoring under tropical environmental conditions where optical imagery alone may be insufficient.

Rather than viewing Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 as competing technologies, recent research increasingly recognizes their complementary strengths. Sentinel-2 effectively captures spectral characteristics associated with vegetation health, whereas Sentinel-1 contributes structural and soil moisture information that remains available despite adverse weather conditions (Fernandez-Beltran et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020). Consequently, combining radar and optical observations has become a common strategy for improving agricultural monitoring. Ramadhani et al. (2020) demonstrated that integrating Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 improved rice growth stage classification compared with single-sensor approaches, while Fikriyah et al. (2025) achieved approximately 92% classification accuracy in rice mapping across several Philippine provinces using multisensor data fusion. Similar findings were reported by Ramadhani et al. (2020), who concluded that multisensor integration produces a more complete representation of crop conditions by combining vegetation information from optical imagery with structural information obtained from radar observations. These studies consistently suggest that integrating Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 reduces the limitations associated with individual sensors and improves the reliability of agricultural monitoring systems.

Beyond improving crop classification and yield estimation, recent studies have also emphasized the importance of increasing the spatial resolution of satellite-derived agricultural information. Conventional satellite products and official agricultural statistics are commonly generated at regional, municipal, or grid-based resolutions that may not adequately represent productivity differences within smaller administrative units. To address this limitation, researchers have developed spatial disaggregation techniques that redistribute coarse-resolution agricultural information into finer geographic units using vegetation indices, crop biophysical variables, and administrative boundaries (Mohanasundaram et al., 2023). By integrating remotely sensed variables such as NDVI, EVI, and Leaf Area Index (LAI), Mohanasundaram et al. (2023) successfully downscaled rice yield estimates from 50-kilometer grids to approximately 500-meter resolution across South and Southeast Asia, substantially improving agreement with observed production statistics. Similarly, Gilardelli et al. (2019) demonstrated that assimilating Sentinel-2-derived LAI into crop growth models enabled sub-field estimation of rice yield variability within individual agricultural fields. However, studies also acknowledge that fragmented agricultural landscapes continue to present challenges for medium-resolution satellite imagery because mixed pixels reduce the accuracy of crop identification in smallholder farming systems (Ginting et al., 2025). Nevertheless, these investigations collectively demonstrate that preserving and utilizing spatial variability is essential for translating remotely sensed agricultural information into geographically meaningful decision-support tools.

Synthesis

The reviewed literature consistently demonstrates that remote sensing has become a reliable and scalable approach for agricultural monitoring by enabling continuous observation of crop conditions across large geographic areas. Sentinel-2 provides valuable multispectral information for assessing vegetation health through indices such as NDVI, EVI, and NDWI, while Sentinel-1 complements these observations by supplying weather-independent radar information related to crop structure and soil moisture (Fernandez-Beltran et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020). Studies further show that integrating Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 significantly improves monitoring accuracy by combining complementary optical and radar observations (Ramadhani et al., 2020; Fikriyah et al., 2025). In addition, advances in spatial disaggregation techniques have demonstrated the feasibility of translating satellite-derived agricultural information into finer geographic units that better represent local production variability (Mohanasundaram et al., 2023; Gilardelli et al., 2019). Despite these advances, most existing studies focus primarily on crop mapping, yield estimation, or regional agricultural assessment, with relatively limited attention given to integrating multisensor remote sensing, barangay-level spatial visualization, and interactive Web-GIS technologies within operational decision-support systems for Local Government Units. The reviewed literature demonstrates that advances in remote sensing, deep learning, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and Web-based decision-support technologies have significantly improved agricultural monitoring and spatial analysis. Recent studies have shown the effectiveness of integrating Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery with CNN-LSTM models for rice yield prediction, while Web-GIS platforms have enhanced the accessibility and interpretation of spatial information for decision-makers. Likewise, Philippine government initiatives and LGU implementations have demonstrated the growing adoption of GIS technologies in local governance to support evidence-based planning and resource management. Despite these developments, limited research has integrated enhanced rice yield prediction, barangay-level spatial visualization, residual error mapping, and role-based data management into a unified Web-GIS platform specifically designed for Local Government Unit agriculture offices. This gap provides the foundation for the present study, which proposes AgriKA-GIS as a spatial decision-support system that combines predictive analytics, interactive geospatial visualization, and secure information management to support barangay-level rice productivity monitoring and agricultural planning in Laguna This gap provides the foundation for the present study, which extends existing remote sensing applications by integrating Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning and Web-GIS technologies to support barangay-level rice productivity monitoring in Laguna.

2.3 Machine Learning Models for Agricultural Remote Sensing

The rapid advancement of remote sensing technologies has been accompanied by the increasing adoption of machine learning and deep learning models for agricultural monitoring and crop yield prediction. These computational approaches enable researchers to analyze complex relationships between remotely sensed imagery, environmental variables, and crop productivity that are difficult to capture using conventional statistical methods. Depending on the characteristics of the data, different models exhibit distinct strengths in extracting spatial, spectral, and temporal information from satellite observations. Consequently, numerous studies have explored various machine learning architectures to improve the accuracy and reliability of agricultural monitoring systems.

Among traditional machine learning approaches, Random Forest (RF) has become one of the most widely applied algorithms in agricultural remote sensing because of its robustness against overfitting, ability to handle high-dimensional datasets, and effectiveness in modeling nonlinear relationships. Choudhary et al. (2022) utilized a Random Forest model with Sentinel-2 imagery and Google Earth Engine to perform rice yield mapping and prediction by integrating spectral information derived from satellite observations. Against Linear Regression and Decision Tree, it achieved more than 85% accuracy. Similarly, Wang et al. (2024) employed geospatial machine learning techniques, including Random Forest, to identify the spatial determinants influencing rice yield across China's major rice-producing regions. The model created proved that Random Forest could handle multiple geographic, climatic, soil, and environmental variables simultaneously, and can capture spatial variability effectively rather than assuming a single global relationship. These studies demonstrate that Random Forest performs well in handling heterogeneous remote sensing datasets and provides interpretable estimates of variable importance. However, the reviewed studies also acknowledge that Random Forest relies heavily on manually engineered features and does not inherently capture temporal crop development throughout an entire growing season. Consequently, although Random Forest serves as an effective baseline model for agricultural prediction, its capability to model sequential crop growth remains limited when compared with deep learning architectures.

Another widely adopted machine learning algorithm is Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), which has gained popularity because of its strong predictive capability, efficient handling of large datasets, and ability to model complex nonlinear relationships. Sah et al. (2024) evaluated XGBoost alongside eight other machine learning algorithms for rice yield prediction using integrated Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), Sentinel-2 optical imagery, and crop biophysical parameters. The study reported that XGBoost consistently achieved the best prediction performance for summer rice across the 45-, 60-, and 90-day after transplanting (DAT) growth stages and also ranked as the best-performing model for the 45 DAT prediction of the kharif season, demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling complex relationships among multisource remote sensing variables. Compared with Random Forest, XGBoost often achieves higher predictive accuracy through gradient boosting optimization and sequential error correction. Nevertheless, the studies emphasize that XGBoost still depends on manually extracted remote sensing features and lacks the capability to automatically learn spatial representations directly from satellite imagery or temporal relationships across multiple observations. As a result, its applicability becomes limited for spatiotemporal agricultural prediction tasks requiring sequential analysis of crop growth.

The increasing availability of high-resolution satellite imagery has also encouraged the adoption of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for agricultural remote sensing because of their ability to automatically learn hierarchical spatial features from images without requiring extensive manual feature engineering. Fernandez-Beltran et al. (2021) developed a three-dimensional CNN (3D CNN) using multi-temporal Sentinel-2 imagery for rice yield prediction in Nepal by capturing both spectral and spatial information from sequential satellite observations. The proposed model achieved the lowest RMSE of 89.03 kg/ha, substantially outperforming conventional regression methods as well as CNN-2D and CNN-3D baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of deep convolutional architectures for extracting spatial and temporal information from multi-temporal satellite imagery. Likewise, Han et al. (2022) proposed a CNN-based image-driven data assimilation framework that integrates handheld RGB images with the ORYZA2000 crop growth model through an Ensemble Kalman Filter for rice yield estimation. The proposed framework achieved an R² of 0.646 and an RMSE of 0.679 t ha⁻¹, outperforming conventional field-sampling assimilation (R² = 0.410, RMSE = 1.059 t ha⁻¹). Additionally, the CNN accurately estimated rice development stages from images, achieving an R² of 0.99 and an RMSE of 2.61, demonstrating the effectiveness of convolutional neural networks in extracting crop phenological information. Similarly, Tanaka et al. (2023) employed a CNN to estimate rice yield directly from more than 22,000 ground-based RGB images collected across six countries in Africa and Japan. The model explained approximately 68% of the variation in rice yield while achieving a relative RMSE of 0.22 and demonstrated robustness under varying lighting conditions, camera angles, and reduced image resolutions, highlighting the ability of CNNs to generalize across diverse agricultural environments. These studies consistently indicate that CNNs effectively identify vegetation patterns, canopy characteristics, and spatial variations associated with crop productivity. However, because convolutional networks primarily process images independently, they have limited capability to represent temporal dependencies between successive crop growth stages. Consequently, CNN-based models alone may not fully capture the dynamic nature of rice development throughout an entire cropping season.

To address the limitations of purely spatial models, researchers have increasingly adopted Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for agricultural applications involving sequential observations. LSTM is a specialized recurrent neural network architecture designed to preserve long-term dependencies within time-series data, making it particularly suitable for modeling crop development across multiple observation dates. Li et al. (2025) proposed an attention-enhanced LSTM (ALSTM) model for early rice yield estimation using Sentinel-2 time-series vegetation indices derived from remotely sensed agricultural observations. The conventional LSTM model achieved an R² of 0.83, RMSE of 451.11 kg ha⁻¹, and MAE of 326.31 kg ha⁻¹, outperforming both LASSO (R² = 0.71, RMSE = 567.10 kg ha⁻¹) and Random Forest (R² = 0.79, RMSE = 506.70 kg ha⁻¹). By incorporating an attention mechanism, the proposed ALSTM further improved prediction performance, achieving an R² of 0.88, RMSE of 341.82 kg ha⁻¹, and MAE of 280.29 kg ha⁻¹, demonstrating the effectiveness of selectively emphasizing the most informative growth stages during the rice growing season. On the other hand, Jeong et al. (2021) integrated an LSTM network with the ORYZA(v3) crop growth model and MODIS satellite observations to predict rice yield at the pixel level across the Korean Peninsula. The proposed framework achieved an R² of 0.84, an RMSE of 0.40 t ha⁻¹, and an MAE of 0.33 t ha⁻¹, outperforming approaches that relied solely on crop growth simulations or satellite observations. These studies demonstrate that LSTM effectively captures seasonal variations and environmental changes affecting crop productivity, resulting in improved modeling of temporal agricultural processes. Nevertheless, LSTM alone cannot effectively extract complex spatial patterns from satellite imagery because it operates primarily on sequential numerical inputs rather than directly learning image representations. This limitation reduces its effectiveness when used independently for remote sensing applications where spatial information is equally important.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have introduced Vision Transformers (ViTs) as an alternative to convolution-based image analysis. Unlike CNNs, Vision Transformers employ self-attention mechanisms that capture long-range spatial relationships across an entire image, enabling more comprehensive contextual understanding. Nejad et al. (2024) proposed a ConvLSTM-ViT architecture that combines convolutional feature extraction, temporal sequence modeling, and transformer-based attention mechanisms for crop yield prediction using Earth observation data. The proposed hybrid model achieved the lowest average RMSE of 6.275 across the evaluation period and attained an RMSE of 6.02, MAE of 3.52, and a correlation coefficient (R) of 0.89 on the 2019 test dataset, outperforming standalone 3D-CNN, ConvLSTM, and previous CNN-LSTM models. Similarly, Inderka et al. (2024) evaluated a Convolutional Vision Transformer (CvT) for crop yield prediction using Sentinel-2 time-series imagery and compared its performance with CNN and XGBoost models. This study found out that CvT effectively captured global contextual information through self-attention mechanisms. Thakkar and Vanzara (2024) also evaluated a Vision Transformer (ViT) for crop yield estimation using MODIS remote sensing imagery of soybean and corn. The ViT achieved R² values ranging from 0.9752 to 0.9875 for soybean and 0.9540 to 0.9888 for corn, with RMSE values between 7.75086 and 9.76838 for soybean and 26.25265 and 34.20382 for corn. The findings demonstrated that self-attention mechanisms enable Vision Transformers to capture global contextual information from remotely sensed imagery while producing highly accurate crop yield estimates without explicit image pre-processing. The reviewed studies indicate that Vision Transformers outperform conventional convolutional models when sufficient training data are available because they effectively model global spatial dependencies. This means that in order to effectively use the model, it requires substantially larger datasets, greater computational resources, and longer training times than CNN-based models. These requirements may reduce their practicality for agricultural applications where labeled remote sensing data remain relatively limited.

While individual architectures such as CNNs and LSTMs have demonstrated strong performance in spatial and temporal learning, respectively, recent studies increasingly recognize that hybrid deep learning models provide a more comprehensive solution by integrating the complementary strengths of multiple architectures. Early work by Khaki et al. (2020) demonstrated this concept by combining convolutional neural networks with recurrent neural networks (CNN-RNN) for crop yield prediction, showing that integrating spatial feature extraction with sequential learning significantly improved predictive performance compared with conventional machine learning models. The proposed framework consistently outperformed Random Forest, Deep Fully Connected Neural Networks (DFNN), and LASSO across the 2016–2018 validation years. For corn yield prediction, the CNN-RNN achieved validation RMSEs of 16.48, 15.74, and 17.64 bushels per acre, with corresponding correlation coefficients of 85.82%, 88.24%, and 87.82%, while for soybean, it obtained RMSEs of 4.15, 4.32, and 4.91 bushels per acre, with correlation coefficients ranging from 85.45% to 87.09%. Overall, the model achieved prediction errors equivalent to only 9% and 8% of the average corn and soybean yields, respectively, demonstrating superior predictive performance and strong generalization to previously unseen environments. Building upon this concept, Lu et al. (2024) developed a CNN-LSTM-Attention framework for predicting maize, rice, and soybean yields using multisource remote sensing and environmental data. For rice yield prediction, the proposed model achieved an R² of 0.991, RMSE of 0.025, and MAE of 0.019, outperforming Random Forest, XGBoost, and conventional CNN models. By integrating convolutional feature extraction, temporal sequence learning, and an attention mechanism, the framework effectively captured complex spatial–temporal relationships within multisource agricultural datasets, demonstrating the advantages of hybrid deep learning architectures for crop yield prediction. Similarly, Jeong et al. (2022) developed a hybrid 1D-CNN + LSTM framework that integrates satellite remote sensing data with a process-based crop model for pixel-scale rice yield prediction across South and North Korea. Their model achieved an R² of 0.859, an RMSE of 0.605 Mg ha⁻¹, and a Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of 0.858, demonstrating reliable rice yield prediction approximately two months before harvest while effectively modeling the spatial and temporal dynamics of crop growth. Zhou et al. (2023) evaluated CNN-LSTM, CNN, and ConvLSTM models for county-level rice yield prediction in Hubei Province, China, using MODIS-derived vegetation indices (EVI, GPP, and SAVI), ERA5 temperature data, and spatial heterogeneity information. The authors reported that the CNN-LSTM model consistently outperformed the standalone CNN, demonstrating that integrating convolutional feature extraction with temporal sequence learning improved prediction accuracy by effectively capturing both spatial variability and crop growth dynamics. Most notably, Ebron et al. (2025) developed the original AgriKA CNN-LSTM model, which integrated Sentinel-2-derived vegetation indices, including NDVI, EVI, and Green Ratio, with meteorological variables to predict rice yield using high-resolution satellite imagery. The optimized CNN-LSTM model achieved an RMSE of 0.5545, MAE of 0.4324, and an R² of 0.3125, demonstrating improved predictive performance following feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, and architectural optimization. By combining multispectral vegetation indices with temporal weather observations, the model effectively learned both spatial and temporal characteristics of rice growth, establishing the baseline framework upon which the present AgriKA-GIS study extends through the integration of Sentinel-1 SAR data, barangay-level spatial analysis, and a Web-GIS decision-support platform. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures effectively combine convolutional feature extraction with temporal sequence learning to capture both the spatial characteristics of remotely sensed imagery and the temporal dynamics of crop development, resulting in more accurate and robust crop yield prediction. Although these hybrid architectures generally require greater computational resources and longer training times than conventional machine learning models, the literature consistently identifies CNN-LSTM as one of the most effective deep learning approaches for satellite-based rice yield prediction because it simultaneously preserves spatial and temporal information. This capability aligns closely with the objectives of AgriKA-GIS, which seeks to enhance rice yield prediction by integrating multisource remote sensing data while supporting barangay-level spatial monitoring and decision-making.

CHAPTER 3

Research Methodology

Research Design

This study employs a Developmental Research Design using a quantitative research approach to develop and evaluate AgriKA-GIS, a Web-based spatial decision-support system for barangay-level rice productivity monitoring in Laguna. Developmental research is appropriate because the study involves the design, development, enhancement, and evaluation of both a software system and a predictive model. As described by Richey and Klein (2007), developmental research focuses on the systematic design, development, and evaluation of products and tools intended to address practical problems. In this study, the products consist of AgriKA-GIS as the decision-support platform and the enhanced AgriKA CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model, which are developed and evaluated to support agricultural monitoring and planning within LGU.

A quantitative research approach is employed because the study relies on numerical data obtained from historical rice yield records, satellite remote sensing imagery, meteorological observations, model prediction outputs, and user evaluation results. Quantitative methods enable the researchers to objectively assess the predictive performance of the enhanced rice yield prediction model and determine the usability and acceptability of the developed Web-based decision-support system through statistical analysis.

The study consists of interrelated development and evaluation components that correspond to the research objectives and collectively support the design, implementation, and assessment of AgriKA-GIS. These components include the enhancement of the existing CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model, the development of a Web-based Geographic Information System (Web-GIS) for barangay-level spatial visualization, the implementation of residual mapping for spatial error analysis, the development of a role-based data management system, and the comprehensive evaluation of the developed platform through predictive performance assessment and User Acceptance Testing (UAT).

The enhanced rice yield prediction model is developed to improve the accuracy and reliability of rice yield forecasting through the integration of Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, meteorological variables, and historical rice yield records. The generated prediction outputs are integrated into the AgriKA-GIS platform, where they are visualized through interactive barangay-level maps and residual error maps to support agricultural monitoring and decision-making.

The completed system is evaluated from both technical and user perspectives. The predictive performance of the enhanced CNN-LSTM model is assessed using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the Coefficient of Determination (R²), while the overall software quality of AgriKA-GIS is evaluated through User Acceptance Testing using the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Quality Model. The completed AgriKA-GIS platform will be evaluated through User Acceptance Testing (UAT) using the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Quality Model. The evaluation will focus on the software quality characteristics most relevant to the proposed system, namely functional suitability, performance efficiency, usability, reliability, security, and maintainability. These characteristics were selected because they assess whether the system performs its intended functions correctly, responds efficiently, protects agricultural data, remains dependable during operation, is easy for intended users to operate, and can be maintained and updated as agricultural monitoring requirements evolve.

Through this developmental research design, the study aims to evaluate both the technical performance of the enhanced rice yield prediction model and the practical usability of AgriKA-GIS as a Web-based spatial decision-support system for LGU agriculture offices in Laguna.

Figure 2. Research Design of the Study

Research Locale

The study was conducted in the Province of Laguna, which served as the geographic scope for rice yield prediction, spatial analysis, and the deployment of the proposed AgriKA-GIS platform. Laguna was selected because it is one of the major rice-producing provinces in the CALABARZON Region and served as the study area of the previous AgriKA project. Retaining the same study area enables direct comparison between the previous and enhanced systems while ensuring methodological consistency, data availability, and stakeholder continuity.

The primary research sites included the City Agriculture Offices of Biñan, Cabuyao, Calamba, and Santa Rosa, which served as the principal locations for requirements gathering, system validation, and UAT. These cities were selected because they maintain active rice production areas and regularly conduct agricultural monitoring and production reporting through their respective LGUs. Their participation ensured that the developed system was evaluated by its intended users within actual operational settings.

The Municipality of Los Baños was also included during the requirements-gathering stage because of its proximity to major agricultural research institutions, including the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB). Consultations conducted with agricultural practitioners and domain experts from these institutions provided valuable technical insights that informed the design of the system, particularly in relation to spatial data management, remote sensing applications, and rice productivity monitoring.

In addition, consultations were conducted with the Provincial Agriculture Office of Laguna in Santa Cruz to obtain information regarding existing agricultural monitoring practices and rice production reporting workflows. The Provincial Agriculture Office also served as an important reference for understanding the consolidation and management of rice production records across the participating LGUs.

Collectively, these research sites provided the necessary operational environment, agricultural expertise, historical production data, and stakeholder participation required for the development and evaluation of AgriKA-GIS as a Web-based spatial decision-support system for barangay-level rice productivity monitoring in Laguna.
