Population of the Study

The population of this study consists of the agricultural personnel directly involved in rice production monitoring, agricultural planning, field validation, reporting, and data management within the participating Local Government Units and the Provincial Agriculture Office of Laguna. These officers are the intended end users of AgriKA-GIS and serve as the respondents for its evaluation. Based on institutional data and stakeholder consultations, the accessible population comprises 26 agricultural personnel drawn from the City Agriculture Offices of Biñan, Cabuyao, Calamba, and Santa Rosa and the Provincial Agriculture Office in Santa Cruz.

Of these, 24 are city-level officers and technicians responsible for the four target cities: one Agricultural Technologist from Biñan; one City Agriculturist, one Rice Manager, one Coordinator, and eleven designated area technicians from Cabuyao; one City Agriculturist, one Supervising Agriculturist, two Senior Agriculturists, three rice technicians, and one Rice Report Officer from Calamba; and one City Agriculturist from Santa Rosa. The remaining two are provincial officers, the Provincial Agriculturist and the Provincial Rice Report Officer, who exercise province-wide oversight and operate the Administrator-level functions of the system.

Local rice farmers are not respondents in the system evaluation. Their reported seasonal harvests instead serve as the ground-level source of the recorded yield data used as ground truth for training and validating the prediction model. The Municipality of Los Baños likewise participated only during the requirements-gathering stage, providing operational and technical insights that informed the system design rather than serving as an evaluation site. This distinction ensures that AgriKA-GIS is evaluated by the LGU and provincial personnel who will actually operate it, while farmer-reported production serves as the observed data against which predictions are compared.

Sampling Techniques

This study will employ purposive sampling through total enumeration (total population sampling), inviting every member of the accessible population to participate rather than drawing a subset. Total enumeration is appropriate because the population is small and every respondent possesses specialized knowledge and direct experience in agricultural monitoring and rice production management; there is therefore no basis for excluding any qualified evaluator (Creswell & Creswell, 2018; Etikan et al., 2016). Accordingly, all 26 agricultural personnel, the City Agriculturists, Rice Technicians, and specialized officers of the four participating City Agriculture Offices, together with the two Provincial Agriculture Office officers, will be invited to participate in the User Acceptance Testing.

The selection of these respondents is based on their direct involvement in rice production monitoring, field validation, agricultural reporting, and decision-making, which makes them the most appropriate evaluators of AgriKA-GIS as its intended end users. The use of a purposively selected expert group is appropriate for developmental research, where the objective is to obtain informed evaluations from individuals with relevant domain expertise rather than to generalize findings to a larger population (Richey & Klein, 2007). This approach is consistent with the previous AgriKA study, which evaluated its system using a small panel of agricultural experts and obtained a Cronbach's Alpha of 0.8442, indicating good internal consistency (Ebron et al., 2025). Similar LGU-based agricultural decision-support studies have likewise adopted purposive sampling, recognizing that the expertise and operational experience of evaluators are more important than sample size in assessing system usability and practical applicability (Panda et al., 2025; Odion et al., 2023).

Data Gathering Tools

The study will utilize both primary and secondary data sources to support the development and evaluation of AgriKA-GIS. Primary data will be collected through stakeholder interviews and UAT, while secondary data will consist of historical rice production records, satellite remote sensing imagery, meteorological information, and geospatial datasets. The integration of these data sources provides the environmental, spatial, and operational information required for enhancing the rice yield prediction model and developing the Web-based spatial decision-support system.

In addition to the collected datasets, the researchers will utilize the original AgriKA study (Ebron et al., 2025) as a documentary reference in the development of AgriKA-GIS. The study will serve as the primary basis for understanding the existing CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model, including its architecture, feature engineering process, data preprocessing techniques, training methodology, and evaluation procedures. Insights obtained from the original study will guide the enhancement of the prediction model through the integration of additional remote sensing data and its incorporation into the proposed Web-GIS platform. By referencing the established methodology of AgriKA, the researchers aim to ensure consistency while extending its capabilities to support barangay-level spatial visualization and decision support.

Structured Stakeholder Interviews

Structured stakeholder interviews will be conducted with City Agriculturists, Rice Technicians, and other authorized personnel from the participating City Agriculture Offices in Biñan, Cabuyao, Calamba, Santa Rosa, and Los Baños. The interview guide will consist of predetermined open-ended questions designed to obtain information regarding existing rice production monitoring practices, agricultural reporting workflows, data management procedures, and the challenges encountered during routine monitoring activities.

The interviews will also be used to identify the functional and non-functional requirements of AgriKA-GIS, including the information needs of agricultural personnel, preferred visualization methods, reporting requirements, and desired system functionalities. Furthermore, stakeholder feedback will be sought to validate the proposed design of the system and ensure that the developed platform aligns with the operational workflow of Local Government Unit (LGU) agriculture offices. According to Hove and Anda (2005), structured interviews provide researchers with consistent and reliable information while allowing practitioners to share operational knowledge that cannot be obtained through documentary sources alone. The responses obtained from these interviews will serve as an important basis for refining the system requirements and validating the relevance of the developed platform.

Remote Sensing Data

Satellite remote sensing imagery will serve as the primary environmental data source for rice yield prediction. The study will utilize Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery and Sentinel-1 SAR imagery, which are freely available through the European Space Agency's Copernicus Programme.

Sentinel-2 imagery will be used to derive vegetation indices that describe crop vigor and vegetation condition throughout the rice growing season. Specifically, the study will utilize the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), and Green Ratio, which have been widely adopted for crop monitoring and rice yield prediction because they provide indicators of vegetation health, biomass, and canopy development (Fernandez-Beltran et al., 2021; Saini & Nagpal, 2024). These vegetation indices will provide spatial information describing rice crop conditions at different stages of growth.

Green Ratio is computed as GR = NIR / Green, where NIR is the near-infrared reflectance band and Green is the green reflectance band captured by Sentinel-2. Green Ratio uses the Green band, which is more sensitive to chlorophyll concentration and canopy density in the earlier and mid-growth stages of the rice crop, compared to NDVI, which contrasts NIR against Red reflectance. A higher Green Ratio indicates denser, healthier vegetation cover. This index is included alongside NDVI and EVI because it provides complementary sensitivity to crop vigor at growth stages where NDVI tends to saturate, thereby improving the model's ability to characterize rice crop conditions used as predictive features for yield estimation.

Complementing the optical imagery, Sentinel-1 SAR data will be utilized to derive soil moisture indicators that represent field conditions regardless of weather or lighting conditions. Unlike optical sensors, Sentinel-1 radar imagery can penetrate cloud cover, making it particularly suitable for monitoring rice fields during the wet season when cloud contamination frequently limits optical observations (Wu et al., 2020). The integration of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 enables the study to utilize complementary environmental information describing vegetation condition and soil moisture, thereby improving the robustness of the rice yield prediction model.

Meteorological Data

Meteorological variables will be obtained through the Open-Meteo API, which provides freely accessible historical and near-real-time weather information. The study will collect environmental variables including rainfall, temperature, and relative humidity, as these factors directly influence rice growth and productivity throughout the cropping season.

The meteorological data will be synchronized with the satellite imagery and historical rice production records to represent the environmental conditions experienced during each cropping period. The use of Open-Meteo eliminates the need for localized weather stations while providing consistent and accessible meteorological information appropriate for agricultural monitoring applications (Ebron et al., 2025). These weather variables will serve as additional inputs to the enhanced rice yield prediction model.

Historical Rice Yield Records

Historical rice production records will serve as the ground truth dataset for model training, validation, and evaluation. Municipal-level seasonal rice yield records will be obtained from the PhilRice, which maintains official production statistics for rice-producing municipalities throughout the country.

To improve the spatial resolution of the study, barangay-level rice production records will also be requested from the participating City Agriculture Offices whenever available. These local production records will supplement the municipal datasets and provide more geographically detailed information for evaluating prediction performance at the barangay level. The historical yield records will be compared with the model-generated predictions to determine prediction accuracy and generate residual maps illustrating spatial prediction errors.

Geospatial Data

Barangay boundary shapefiles for the Province of Laguna will be obtained from publicly available geospatial repositories and validated through consultations with the Provincial Agriculture Office. These shapefiles contain the geographic boundaries of the barangays included in the study area and provide the spatial framework for the AgriKA-GIS platform.

The geospatial datasets will be used to visualize predicted rice yields, residual maps, and other spatial information generated by the developed system. By linking prediction outputs with barangay polygons, AgriKA-GIS will transform numerical prediction results into interactive geographic visualizations that support agricultural monitoring and spatial decision-making.

User Acceptance Testing (UAT) Questionnaire

The usability and acceptability of AgriKA-GIS will be evaluated using a structured UAT developed based on the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Quality Model. The questionnaire will measure the respondents' assessment of the developed system based on the selected ISO/IEC 25010 software quality characteristics, namely functional suitability, performance efficiency, usability, reliability, security, and maintainability. These quality characteristics are considered the most appropriate for evaluating the effectiveness and overall acceptability of AgriKA-GIS as a Web-based spatial system. .

Each statement will be rated using a four-point Likert scale, ranging from Strongly Disagree (1) to Strongly Agree (4). The evaluation instrument is adapted from the previous AgriKA study (Ebron et al., 2025) to maintain consistency in assessing user acceptance and to facilitate comparison between the previous and enhanced systems. The completed questionnaires will provide quantitative evidence regarding the overall usability, effectiveness, and acceptability of AgriKA-GIS as a Web-based spatial decision-support system.

Data Gathering Procedure

The data gathering process will be conducted in five sequential phases to ensure the systematic collection of both primary and secondary data required for the development and evaluation of AgriKA-GIS.

Phase 1. Stakeholder Coordination and Requirements Gathering

The researchers will first secure approval from the participating City Agriculture Offices and the Provincial Agriculture Office before conducting stakeholder consultations. Structured interviews will then be administered to City Agriculturists and Rice Technicians to document existing agricultural monitoring workflows, reporting procedures, operational challenges, and user requirements. The information gathered during this phase will guide the refinement of the system requirements and ensure that AgriKA-GIS addresses the practical needs of its intended users.

Phase 2. Collection of Secondary Datasets

Following the completion of stakeholder consultations, the researchers will collect the secondary datasets required for the study. Historical rice production records will be obtained from PhilRice and the participating LGU, while Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, meteorological data from the Open-Meteo API, and barangay boundary shapefiles will be acquired from their respective publicly available sources. These datasets will be reviewed to ensure completeness, consistency, and suitability for subsequent analysis.

Phase 3. Data Preparation

Satellite Image Selection and Growth-Stage Assignment

Sentinel-2 has a revisit interval of approximately five days, producing many acquisitions over a single cropping cycle. Using every available image indiscriminately would introduce redundant and stage-ambiguous observations into the prediction model. This study therefore applies a structured image-selection procedure that filters Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 acquisitions and assigns each retained image to a specific rice growth stage, so that the temporal sequence supplied to the CNN-LSTM model represents the crop's phenological development rather than an arbitrary five-day series.

Because planting in the study area is staggered rather than synchronized, as confirmed during stakeholder interviews, where agricultural officers reported that fields within a city are transplanted at different times across the season, image selection cannot rely on fixed calendar dates alone. Two fields imaged on the same date may be at entirely different growth stages. Each cropping cycle is therefore anchored to its reported planting or harvest date, and growth stages are identified from the temporal trajectory of vegetation indices computed from the imagery itself. The selection procedure consists of the following steps.

1. Definition of the cropping window. Each cropping cycle is bounded using the season's planting-to-harvest period. Following the IRRI month-based seasonal categorization, the dry-season (first-semester) crop is generally harvested around March–April and the wet-season (second-semester) crop around September–October, with maturity occurring roughly 110–136 days after sowing depending on variety. The specific window for each barangay-season is aligned to the planting and harvest dates reported by the City Agriculture Office, accommodating the staggered planting observed in the study area.

2. Retrieval and cloud filtering. All Sentinel-2 acquisitions within the cropping window over the barangay area of interest are retrieved. Each image is screened using its scene-classification and cloud mask, and acquisitions in which cloud or cloud-shadow contamination exceeds a defined threshold over the rice-paddy pixels are discarded. Sentinel-1 SAR acquisitions, which penetrate cloud cover, are retained over the same window to provide continuity during periods when optical imagery is unusable, most notably during the wet season, when persistent cloud cover frequently limits Sentinel-2 observations.

3. Index computation. For each retained Sentinel-2 image, NDVI, EVI, and Green Ratio are computed over the rice-paddy pixels and summarized (e.g., by mean value) for the area of interest, producing a time-ordered series of index values across the cropping cycle.

4. Growth-stage assignment from the index trajectory. The ordered index series describes the characteristic rice phenological curve: low values shortly after transplanting (exposed water and soil), a rising limb during the vegetative stage, a peak at the reproductive stage, and a declining limb during ripening toward harvest. Each image is assigned to one of the four growth stages, newly planted, vegetative, reproductive, and harvest, according to where its index value falls along this trajectory, using the stage thresholds. The maximum of the curve identifies the reproductive stage, while the harvest-stage image is the acquisition on the descending limb closest to the reported harvest date.

5. Selection of representative images. For each growth stage, the least cloud-contaminated image satisfying that stage's index criteria is selected as the representative observation, together with its temporally nearest Sentinel-1 SAR acquisition. These stage-representative images form the temporal input sequence (timesteps) supplied to the CNN-LSTM model, ensuring that each cropping cycle is represented by one clean observation per growth stage rather than by the full five-day series.

Because independent field confirmation of growth stage is not available for every barangay and cycle, and because the harvest date is known from LGU reporting, the NDVI and Green Ratio trajectories serve as the ground-truth proxy for stage assignment: the reported harvest date fixes the timing of the final stage, and the index curve establishes the sequence of preceding stages relative to it. The harvest-stage image is treated as the primary observation for yield labeling, as it corresponds to the point at which rice yield is reported by the City Agriculture Office.

Figure 3. AgriKA-GIS Complete Pipeline Diagram

Image Pre-processing

Before feature extraction, all selected Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 images undergo a pre-processing sequence to ensure spatial consistency, remove invalid observations, and produce comparable inputs across dates and sensors. The previous AgriKA study likewise applied a pre-processing stage, masking invalid pixels through a black-pixel-ratio function and deriving Green Ratio from NDVI imagery, so this study documents its own pre-processing procedure adapted to the integration of Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 optical data. The steps are as follows.

1. Source products. Sentinel-2 imagery is obtained as Level-2A products, which are already atmospherically corrected to surface reflectance, while Sentinel-1 imagery is obtained as Ground Range Detected (GRD) products. Using analysis-ready product levels avoids introducing inconsistencies from manual atmospheric correction.

2. Clipping to the area of interest. Each image is clipped to the barangay boundary polygon obtained from the boundary shapefile, producing a consistent spatial extent per barangay so that observations across different dates and sensors cover exactly the same area.

3. Resampling and co-registration. The Sentinel-2 bands used to compute the vegetation indices are resampled to a common 10-meter ground resolution, and the Sentinel-1 GRD imagery is terrain-corrected (orthorectified) and resampled onto the same 10-meter grid. This aligns the optical and radar observations pixel-for-pixel over each barangay, allowing vegetation indices and SAR-derived indicators to be combined consistently.

4. Masking of invalid pixels. Cloud, cloud-shadow, and no-data (black) pixels are identified using the Sentinel-2 scene-classification and cloud masks together with a no-data mask, and are excluded from all subsequent computation. This ensures that index values are derived only from valid observations of the rice-paddy area, consistent with the masking approach used in the previous study.

5. Standardization of image properties. To keep pixel-based measures comparable across acquisitions, particularly the Green Ratio, which is computed from the proportion of green pixels within an image, all clipped rasters for a given barangay are standardized to the same dimensions, spatial resolution, and coordinate reference system.

6. Index computation. From the masked, resampled Sentinel-2 rasters, the NDVI, EVI, and Green Ratio are computed; from the Sentinel-1 rasters, the VV and VH backscatter and the derived soil-moisture indicators are computed. Each pre-processed image therefore yields a set of index layers describing vegetation condition and soil moisture for the barangay at that acquisition.

7. Handling of unusable acquisitions. Where cloud contamination leaves a growth stage without a valid Sentinel-2 image, the temporally nearest Sentinel-1 SAR observation preserves coverage for that stage; any remaining gaps in the resulting feature series are addressed during feature engineering through imputation, so that each cropping cycle retains a complete stage sequence.

The pre-processed images produce analysis-ready index values for each barangay and growth stage, which are then passed to the Feature Engineering and Data Preparation stage for imputation, normalization, and organization into the temporal sequences supplied to the CNN-LSTM model.

Enhanced CNN-LSTM Model Development

Following data preparation, the researchers will develop an enhanced Convolutional Neural Network–Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) model for barangay-level rice yield prediction. The enhanced model extends the previous AgriKA CNN-LSTM architecture by incorporating Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)-derived features together with Sentinel-2 multispectral vegetation indices, meteorological variables, and historical rice yield records to improve prediction robustness under varying environmental conditions.

Data Dictionary

To ensure that only informative and non-redundant variables are retained as inputs to the prediction model, a feature-selection step will be performed prior to model training. The candidate predictors, the Sentinel-2 vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI, and Green Ratio), the Sentinel-1 SAR-derived soil-moisture indicators (VV and VH polarizations), and the meteorological variables (rainfall, temperature, and relative humidity), will each be assessed for their contribution to predicting rice yield.

The relevance of each candidate feature will be evaluated using Information Gain, which measures the reduction in uncertainty about the yield outcome attributable to knowledge of that feature. For this assessment, recorded rice yield will be discretized into ordered productivity categories so that Information Gain can be computed, while the final prediction model continues to estimate yield as a continuous value. Features contributing little information about the yield outcome will be considered for removal, and those providing substantial, complementary discriminative value will be retained.

This step also serves to verify that the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) is not redundant with the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI). Because EVI is mathematically related to and partly derived from the same near-infrared and red reflectance bands as NDVI, their individual Information Gain values relative to the yield outcome will be compared directly. EVI will be retained as a separate predictor only if it contributes information beyond that already captured by NDVI; otherwise it will be excluded to avoid redundancy. The resulting set of retained variables constitutes the final attribute list used by the prediction model, presented in Table 5.

Data Collection

Figure 4. AgriKA Data Collection

Figure 5. AgriKA-GIS Data Collection

Feature Engineering and Data Preparation

Before the datasets are used for feature extraction and rice yield prediction, they undergo a series of preprocessing steps to improve their quality, consistency, and compatibility. Historical rice yield records are cleaned by handling missing values, detecting outliers, validating barangay and municipality information, standardizing dates, and aligning records with the appropriate cropping season. Sentinel-2 optical images are preprocessed through cloud masking, atmospheric correction, image clipping, resizing, normalization, and the computation of vegetation indices such as NDVI, EVI, and Green Ratio. Similarly, Sentinel-1 SAR images undergo orbit correction, thermal noise removal, radiometric calibration, speckle filtering, terrain correction, and the extraction of VV and VH backscatter features. Meteorological data from Open-Meteo are cleaned, aggregated, synchronized with the satellite acquisition dates, and normalized, while barangay shapefiles are validated and processed to ensure accurate spatial alignment with the other datasets. Then, all data sources are integrated into a single unified dataset through feature scaling, temporal alignment, spatial matching, and consistency checking. This process ensures that satellite imagery, weather variables, historical rice yield records, and spatial information correspond to the same barangays and cropping periods while minimizing errors caused by missing, inconsistent, or misaligned data. The resulting preprocessed dataset provides a standardized and reliable input for the ResNet50 feature extraction stage and the enhanced CNN-LSTM model, enabling more accurate barangay-level rice yield prediction and spatial visualization.

Figure 6. Data Preprocessing

CNN-LSTM Architecture

The enhanced prediction model consists of two primary components:

- Convolutional Neural Network (CNN): The CNN extracts spatial features from remotely sensed variables, learning relationships among vegetation indices, SAR-derived measurements, and environmental variables that characterize rice growth conditions.

- Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM): The extracted spatial features are subsequently processed by an LSTM network, which captures temporal dependencies across multiple observation periods within the cropping season. This enables the model to learn changes in crop development over time and their relationship to final rice yield.

The output layer consists of a fully connected regression layer that predicts continuous rice yield values for each barangay.

Model Training

The prepared dataset will be divided into three subsets:

- 70% Training Set – used for model learning;

- 15% Validation Set – used for hyperparameter tuning and monitoring model performance during training; and

- 15% Testing Set – reserved for final model evaluation using previously unseen data.

The model will be trained using the Adam optimizer, which is widely used for deep learning regression tasks because of its computational efficiency and adaptive learning capability. A learning rate of 0.001 will be used as the initial optimization parameter.

Training will be performed using a batch size of 32 over a maximum of 100 epochs. The Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function will be employed to minimize the difference between predicted and observed rice yield values.

Hyperparameter Tuning and Model Validation

To obtain the optimal prediction model, selected hyperparameters, including the number of LSTM units, number of convolutional filters, dropout rate, batch size, and learning rate, will be adjusted through iterative experimentation using the validation dataset. The model configuration that produces the lowest validation error will be selected for final testing.

To reduce overfitting, an Early Stopping mechanism will be implemented. Training will automatically terminate if the validation loss does not improve after 10 consecutive epochs, and the model weights corresponding to the best validation performance will be retained.

Model Output

The trained CNN-LSTM model will generate continuous rice yield predictions for each barangay included in the study. These predicted values will subsequently be integrated into the AgriKA-GIS platform for visualization through barangay-level heatmaps and residual error maps. The predictive performance of the final model will then be evaluated using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the Coefficient of Determination (R²), and compared with the previous AgriKA CNN-LSTM model.

Phase 4. System Evaluation

After the development of AgriKA-GIS, the researchers will conduct User Acceptance Testing with the participating City Agriculturists and Rice Technicians. Respondents will be given an orientation on the objectives and functionalities of the system, followed by a demonstration of its major features. Participants will then be allowed to interact with the system independently to perform representative monitoring tasks before completing the evaluation questionnaire.

Phase 5. Collection and Organization of Evaluation Data

Completed questionnaires will be collected immediately after the evaluation session to ensure a high response rate and to allow respondents to provide feedback while their experience with the system remains current. The responses will be encoded, verified for completeness, and organized for statistical analysis. The resulting data will be used to determine the usability, acceptability, and overall effectiveness of AgriKA-GIS as a Web-based spatial decision-support system for barangay-level rice productivity monitoring.

Data Analysis

The data collected in this study will be analyzed using descriptive, inferential, and model evaluation techniques according to the specific objectives of the study. The order of analysis follows the order of the stated objectives to maintain consistency.

Objective 1

To develop and evaluate an extended CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model by integrating Sentinel-1 SAR-derived information with Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, meteorological variables, and historical rice yield data for barangay-level rice yield prediction in Laguna.

The predictive performance of the enhanced CNN-LSTM model will be evaluated using the following regression performance metrics: Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the Coefficient of Determination (R²).

Table 4

Model Evaluation Metrics for Rice Yield Prediction

MetricFormulaWhat It MeasuresInterpretation
Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)√(Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² / n)Average magnitude of prediction error while giving greater weight to larger errorsLower values indicate better predictive accuracy.
Mean Absolute Error (MAE)Σ\yᵢ − ŷᵢ\/ nAverage absolute difference between predicted and observed rice yieldLower values indicate better predictive accuracy.
Coefficient of Determination (R²)1 − (Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² / Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)²)Proportion of variance in observed rice yield explained by the modelValues closer to 1 indicate a better model fit.

where yᵢ = observed rice yield, ŷᵢ = predicted rice yield, ȳ = mean observed yield, and n = total number of observations. Lower RMSE and MAE values and a higher R² value indicate better predictive performance.

To ensure data integrity and provide an objective, holistic assessment of the CNN-LSTM model's predictive performance, this study introduces a Normalized Composite Accuracy Index (NCAI). Traditional evaluation approaches often rely on isolated, rule-based metric checks, which can inadvertently introduce selection bias by favoring a model that performs well in one specific area (e.g., minimizing absolute error) while underperforming in another (e.g., variance explanation). The NCAI mitigates this by mathematically combining the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the Coefficient of Determination (R^2) into a single, comparable value ranging from 0 to 1, where 1 represents optimal predictive accuracy.

Because these three metrics operate on fundamentally different scales, they must first be normalized. The error metrics, RMSE and MAE, are inverted using Min-Max scaling across all experimental trials so that a higher normalized value correctly reflects a lower error magnitude:

The R^2 value, which represents the model's goodness-of-fit, is standardized to ensure that severe negative values (indicating poor model fit) do not disproportionately skew the composite score:

The final NCAI is calculated as an equally weighted average of the three normalized metrics, ensuring that no single metric dictates the model's overall evaluation:

This unified index serves as the definitive, singular benchmark for ranking the model trials. By evaluating the models based on the NCAI, the study avoids cherry-picking favorable metrics and ensures that the final selected architecture provides the most balanced and statistically sound rice yield forecasts.

Paired Statistical Analysis

To determine whether the enhanced CNN-LSTM model significantly improves prediction performance compared with the previous AgriKA model, the prediction errors generated by both models will be compared using paired statistical analysis. For each observation in the testing dataset (i.e., each barangay-season yield record), the prediction error of the previous AgriKA CNN-LSTM model and the corresponding prediction error of the enhanced CNN-LSTM model will be computed by comparing their predicted rice yield values with the same observed (ground-truth) rice yield. These paired prediction errors represent two measurements obtained from the same observation and serve as the basis for statistical comparison.

Prior to hypothesis testing, the distribution of the paired differences between the prediction errors of the two models will be assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk Test for normality. If the paired differences satisfy the assumption of normality, a paired t-test will be performed to determine whether the enhanced model produces significantly lower prediction errors than the previous AgriKA model. If the normality assumption is violated, the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test will be used as the non-parametric alternative. A significance level of α = 0.05 will be adopted; a computed p-value less than 0.05 will indicate a statistically significant improvement in the predictive performance of the enhanced CNN-LSTM model over the previous AgriKA model.

Objective 2

To develop and evaluate a Web-based spatial decision-support system for barangay-level rice productivity monitoring in Laguna that enables visualization of predicted rice yields, residual maps, and spatial productivity trends to support agricultural monitoring and evidence-based decision-making by Local Government Unit (LGU) agriculture offices.

The developed system will be evaluated through User Acceptance Testing (UAT) using a structured questionnaire based on the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Quality Model. The evaluation will focus on the software quality characteristics most relevant to the proposed system: functional suitability, performance efficiency, usability, reliability, security, and maintainability. Because role-based access control and secure, municipality-specific data management are integral features of the system rather than a separate deliverable, their effectiveness is assessed within this same evaluation, particularly under the functional suitability and security characteristics, confirming that authorized users can access only the information relevant to their role and jurisdiction.

The responses will be summarized using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and standard deviation. The weighted mean will be computed using:

where WM = weighted mean, f = frequency, x = assigned scale value, and N = total number of responses. The resulting mean scores will be interpreted using the following scale:

The reliability of the evaluation instrument will also be assessed using Cronbach's Alpha, where a coefficient of 0.70 or higher indicates acceptable internal consistency (Taber, 2018).

In addition to user evaluation, the system's residual maps will be assessed through spatial error analysis. Residual values will be computed as the difference between the observed and predicted rice yield for each barangay:

eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ

where positive residual values indicate that the model underpredicted rice yield and negative residual values indicate that the model overpredicted rice yield. The computed residuals will be visualized using barangay-level thematic maps within AgriKA-GIS and analyzed descriptively to identify spatial patterns of prediction error and locate areas where the model consistently overestimates or underestimates rice productivity. This analysis complements the numerical performance metrics by providing a geographic interpretation of the model's prediction accuracy.

Objective 3

To develop and evaluate a secure automated data pipeline for acquiring, processing, integrating, and managing Sentinel-1 SAR imagery, Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, meteorological variables, and historical rice yield data to support barangay-level rice yield prediction and spatial visualization.

The data pipeline will be evaluated based on its ability to reliably acquire, preprocess, integrate, and deliver the datasets required for rice yield prediction and spatial visualization, with particular emphasis on automation, that is, the extent to which newly available Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and meteorological data are ingested, processed, and made available to the prediction model and dashboard without manual intervention. Evaluation will be conducted through functional and reliability testing across repeated update cycles, verifying successful automated acquisition from the Copernicus and Open-Meteo sources, correct computation of vegetation indices and SAR-derived indicators, accurate integration into the PostgreSQL/PostGIS spatial database, and consistent delivery of prepared data to downstream components. Data integrity and consistency checks will be applied at each stage to confirm that records remain complete, correctly aligned to the cropping calendar and barangay boundaries, and free of loss or duplication throughout the workflow.

Software Design

This section presents the system design of AgriKA-GIS, including the software development methodology, system architecture, major system modules, data flow, database design, and user interface design. The system design explains how the proposed Web-GIS platform will be developed to support barangay-level rice productivity monitoring, spatial visualization, residual mapping, and role-based data management.

Software Development Life Cycle

The development of AgriKA-GIS will follow the Agile Software Development Life Cycle. Agile is selected because the proposed system requires continuous refinement based on feedback from City Agriculturists, Rice Technicians, and other agricultural stakeholders. Since AgriKA-GIS is intended for actual Local Government Unit operations, stakeholder involvement is necessary throughout development to ensure that the system remains aligned with existing monitoring workflows and user needs.

The Agile approach will allow the researchers to develop the system in iterative cycles. Each cycle will involve planning, designing, developing, testing, and refining system features until the platform satisfies the requirements of the intended users. Rather than following a single linear sequence, the process will repeat in short cycles so that feedback from one iteration is incorporated into the next.

As illustrated in Figure 3, the development of AgriKA-GIS will be organized into six iterative Agile phases: Requirements Gathering, System Planning and Design, Development, Testing and Refinement, Deployment and Evaluation, and Review and Feedback. The cyclical arrangement emphasizes that these phases are not performed only once; feedback gathered during evaluation and review will inform further refinement of the system in subsequent iterations.

Figure 7. Agile Software Development Lifecycle

Agile Development Phases

1. Requirements Gathering

In this phase, the researchers will gather system requirements through interviews and consultations with City Agriculturists, Rice Technicians, and agricultural experts. The researchers will identify the users' current monitoring practices, reporting procedures, data needs, and preferred system features. The output of this phase will be a list of functional and non-functional requirements that will guide the development of AgriKA-GIS.

2. System Planning and Design

In this phase, the researchers will design the overall structure of AgriKA-GIS. This includes the system architecture, user roles, database structure, data flow, Web-GIS interface, and visualization features. The researchers will also design how predicted rice yield values, barangay boundaries, residual values, and user account information will be organized within the system.

3. Development

In this phase, the researchers will develop the major components of AgriKA-GIS. These consist of its six system modules: Home and System Information; Real-Time and Historical Yield Monitoring; Spatial GIS Visualization and Analysis; Rice Yield Analytics and Comparison; Reports Generation and Data Import/Export; and User Access Management and System Configuration. The enhanced rice yield prediction outputs will be connected to the Web-GIS platform so that predicted rice productivity can be visualized geographically.

4. Testing and Refinement

In this phase, each system function will be tested to determine whether it performs according to the identified requirements. The researchers will check whether the maps load properly, filters work correctly, residual maps display accurate values, and user access is properly restricted according to role. Feedback from stakeholders will be used to revise and improve the system before final evaluation.

5. Deployment and Evaluation

In this phase, the completed AgriKA-GIS system will be presented to the intended users for evaluation. City Agriculturists and Rice Technicians will interact with the system and assess its usability, functionality, reliability, security, and overall acceptability using the ISO/IEC 25010-based User Acceptance Testing questionnaire.

6. Review and Feedback

In this phase, the results of the evaluation will be reviewed together with feedback from the intended users. Rather than repeating the formal testing, this phase will consolidate the findings to identify remaining limitations and improvements, which will be documented as recommendations for future development and study.

System Architecture

Figure 6 presents the overall system architecture of AgriKA-GIS, which follows a three-tier architecture consisting of the Data Tier, Logic Tier, and Presentation Tier. The architecture integrates multiple agricultural data sources, machine learning, spatial database technologies, and Web-GIS components to support barangay-level rice productivity monitoring and spatial decision-making. By separating data management, application processing, and user interaction into distinct layers, the architecture promotes modularity, maintainability, scalability, and efficient processing of geospatial information.

Figure 8. AgriKA-GIS System Architecture of the Proposed Systems

Data Sources

AgriKA-GIS integrates data from four primary sources that provide the environmental, agricultural, and spatial information required for rice yield prediction and visualization. Satellite imagery is acquired through the Sentinel Hub API, which provides Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery used to derive environmental features relevant to rice productivity. Historical weather variables, including temperature, rainfall, and humidity, are retrieved from the Open-Meteo API to represent the climatic conditions experienced during each cropping season. Historical rice yield records obtained from PhilRice serve as the ground-truth data for model training and evaluation, while Philippine Standard Geographic Code (PSGC) barangay shapefiles provide the administrative boundaries required for barangay-level spatial visualization.

Data Tier

The collected datasets are managed within the Data Tier, which consists of PostgreSQL and its PostGIS extension. PostgreSQL functions as the central relational database that stores agricultural records, historical yield data, prediction results, user information, and other system data. The PostGIS extension extends PostgreSQL with spatial capabilities by supporting geographic data storage, spatial indexing, coordinate reference system transformations, and spatial queries. Barangay boundary shapefiles are stored as GeoJSON-compatible spatial objects, allowing the system to efficiently retrieve and process geographic information for visualization and analysis. The use of PostGIS enables AgriKA-GIS to integrate non-spatial agricultural records with geographic features within a unified spatial database.

Logic Tier

The Logic Tier contains the core processing components responsible for handling user requests, generating predictions, processing spatial information, and managing user access.

The Flask backend serves as the application's server-side component, processing requests from users, coordinating communication between the database and the prediction model, and delivering processed information to the Web-GIS interface. The backend also manages data retrieval, filtering, authentication, and other application services required by the system.

Rice yield prediction is performed by the enhanced CNN-LSTM model, which processes remotely sensed, meteorological, and historical agricultural data to generate predicted rice yield values. These prediction outputs are subsequently processed by the Spatial Query Engine, which performs coordinate transformations, spatial joins, and geographic indexing using PostGIS functions. Through these spatial operations, the predicted yield values are linked to their corresponding barangay boundaries, enabling accurate visualization of rice productivity at the barangay level.

The Logic Tier also incorporates a Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) mechanism that regulates user authentication and authorization. Three user roles are supported: Administrator, Agriculturist, and Rice Technician. The Administrator operates at the provincial level and holds province-wide oversight, including user and account management, system configuration, and the consolidation of municipal yield records for cross-municipality comparison and province-wide reporting. In contrast, agriculturists and rice technicians are granted access only to the data of their assigned city or municipal Agriculture Office, so that local users retrieve and manage agricultural information relevant only to their own jurisdiction. This arrangement protects sensitive system data from unauthorized access while reflecting the actual reporting hierarchy, in which municipal offices consolidate records that are ultimately compiled at the Provincial Agriculture Office.

Presentation Tier

The Presentation Tier provides the user interface through which agricultural personnel interact with AgriKA-GIS. The system utilizes Leaflet.js to present interactive barangay-level heatmaps and residual maps, allowing users to visualize the spatial distribution of predicted rice yields and identify areas with prediction errors. These map-based visualizations transform numerical prediction outputs into geographically meaningful information that supports agricultural monitoring and planning.

In addition to the interactive maps, AgriKA-GIS provides a Yield Dashboard that summarizes historical and current rice productivity through graphical and statistical displays. The dashboard enables users to review rice yield information across different municipalities and cropping seasons, facilitating comparison and trend analysis. The system also includes a Report Export module that allows authorized users to generate reports in PDF, Excel, and CSV formats for documentation, reporting, and decision-making purposes.

End Users

AgriKA-GIS is designed to support three categories of users with varying levels of system access. The Administrator, operating at the provincial level, is responsible for managing system configuration, user accounts, and the consolidation of municipal yield records into province-wide summaries and reports. Agriculturists use the system to monitor rice productivity, evaluate spatial patterns, and support agricultural planning within their assigned city or municipality. Rice Technicians examine barangay-level yield information, validate field conditions, and encode and submit barangay yield records for their assigned area. Guests are provided limited, read-only access to publicly available rice productivity maps and reports.

Through the integration of multisource environmental data, machine learning, spatial database technologies, and interactive Web-GIS visualization, AgriKA-GIS provides a unified spatial decision-support platform that enables Local Government Units to monitor rice productivity, visualize spatial trends, evaluate prediction reliability, and support evidence-based agricultural planning at the barangay level.

Major System Modules

AgriKA-GIS is organized into six major modules that correspond to the core functions of the system. Together, these modules support barangay-level rice productivity monitoring, spatial visualization, analytics, reporting, and secure data access for LGU agriculture offices.

1. Home and System Information Module

This module serves as the entry point of AgriKA-GIS. It presents an overview of the system, including its purpose, main features, and general information on how the platform supports barangay-level rice productivity monitoring in Laguna. From this module, users can navigate to the other modules and view summary information about the system and the participating cities. It provides an accessible starting point and helps orient users to the platform's capabilities.

2. Real-Time and Historical Yield Monitoring Module

This module allows users to monitor rice yield based on the most recent satellite-derived predictions as well as historical yield records. Because Sentinel imagery is updated at regular intervals, the module presents up-to-date predicted rice yield alongside previously recorded production data, enabling users to observe changes in productivity over time. It supports routine monitoring by giving City Agriculturists and Rice Technicians a continuously updated view of rice productivity within their jurisdictions.

3. Spatial GIS Visualization and Analysis Module

This module is the core spatial component of AgriKA-GIS. It displays predicted rice yield through interactive barangay-level heatmaps and presents residual maps that highlight areas where the model over-predicts or under-predicts rice yield relative to recorded data. Users can filter the displayed information by city, barangay, year, and cropping season to examine productivity for specific locations and time periods. By transforming numerical predictions into interactive geographic visualizations, this module supports the main purpose of AgriKA-GIS and helps users identify spatial patterns and barangays that may require field validation.

4. Rice Yield Analytics and Comparison Module

This module provides analytical tools that allow users to compare rice productivity across barangays, cities, and cropping seasons. Through charts, tables, and summary statistics, users can review yield trends, compare predicted and recorded yields, and examine differences in productivity over time. It complements the spatial visualizations by enabling users to interpret rice yield information analytically in support of evidence-based planning.

5. Reports Generation and Data Import/Export Module

This module enables authorized users to generate reports and manage the movement of data into and out of the system. Reports summarizing rice yield information can be exported in PDF, Excel, and CSV formats for documentation, reporting, and decision-making. The module also supports importing relevant agricultural records, allowing the system to be updated as new information becomes available. It improves the accessibility and reusability of rice yield information for LGU operations.

6. User Access Management and System Configuration Module

This module manages user accounts, authentication, and role-based access control. Users are assigned one of three roles, administrator, agriculturist, rice technician, or guest, and access to system functions and data is determined by the assigned role and municipality. Administrators can manage user accounts, maintain agricultural records, and configure system settings, while other users are restricted to information relevant to their responsibilities and jurisdiction. This module ensures secure, municipality-specific access and protects sensitive system data from unauthorized use.

Figure. AgriKA-GIS System Architecture.

Data Flow Design

The system will begin with the collection and preparation of satellite imagery, meteorological data, historical yield records, and barangay boundary data. These datasets will be processed and used by the enhanced prediction model to generate rice yield estimates.

The predicted yield values will then be linked to barangay boundary data and stored in the spatial database. When a user accesses the Web-GIS platform, the system will retrieve the relevant spatial and yield information based on the user's selected filters and access permissions. The results will be displayed as heatmaps, residual maps, charts, or tables.

The general data flow is as follows:

1. Collection of rice yield records, satellite imagery, weather data, and barangay boundaries

2. Data preprocessing and model input preparation

3. Rice yield prediction generation

4. Storage of prediction outputs and spatial data

5. Retrieval of data through the Web-GIS platform

6. Visualization through heatmaps, residual maps, dashboards, and reports

7. User evaluation and feedback for system refinement

Figure 9. Data Flow Diagram

Database Design

The AgriKA-GIS database will store both spatial and non-spatial data. The spatial data will include barangay boundaries and geographic coordinates, while the non-spatial data will include rice yield records, predicted yield values, residual values, user accounts, roles, and system logs.

The main database entities may include:

- Users – stores user account information and assigned roles

- Roles – defines access privileges for each user type

- Municipalities – stores city or municipality information

- Barangays – stores barangay names and spatial boundaries

- Yield Records – stores recorded rice yield data

- Predictions – stores model-generated yield predictions

- Residuals – stores computed prediction errors

- Seasons – stores cropping season and year information

This database structure will allow the system to organize rice yield information by location, season, and user access level.

Figure 10. Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD)

Figure. AgriKA-GIS Database Schema (Entity-Relationship Diagram).

User Profile

Figure 11. Use Case Diagram

The system is designed for three primary user groups: Administrator, Agriculturists, and Rice Technicians, each with specific functions and access privileges suited to their roles in the agricultural monitoring process. To maintain data privacy and system integrity, the platform enforces strict role-based access control, granting the provincial-level Administrator broad oversight across all participating municipalities while restricting local field users and public guests to their assigned jurisdictions or public-facing data streams.

1. Administrator: The Administrator role serves as the highest level of system oversight, focusing on governance, system security, and user account management. As illustrated in Figure 8, these users are responsible for managing the credentials and security of the platform by overseeing user accounts, which includes the explicit authority to manage user accounts, configure core system settings, and assign roles and municipality access. A critical function of the Administrator is securing access control by verifying users before they connect to the main portal. In addition to system configuration, they oversee the macro-level provincial dataset by accepting municipal yield records, managing municipal yield records, generating comparison heatmaps between municipalities, and generating province-wide yield performance reports.

2. Agriculturists: These users function as local city or municipal-level agricultural heads who supervise data collections and review localized yield trends. As shown in Figure 7, they log into the secure portal to access analytical overviews through the municipality dashboard and view barangay yield predictions. Their core operational responsibilities include comparing barangay yield reports, which automatically includes generating yield heatmaps to evaluate production patterns across different agricultural sectors. To communicate field outcomes up the administrative chain, they possess the authority to generate performance reports, which includes exporting location-specific data into downloadable PDF or CSV formats.

3. Rice Technicians: These users function as local city or municipal-level agricultural technologists who handle day-to-day data management and monitoring inside their specific geographic assignments. They log into the secure portal to view their municipality dashboard, view barangay yield predictions, and manage local agricultural records. Their core operational responsibilities include encoding and submitting barangay yield reports directly into the spatial system.

User Interface Design

The user interface of AgriKA-GIS is organized around six major modules, each serving a distinct function aligned with the operational needs of City Agriculturists, Rice Technicians, and other authorized LGU personnel. The interface is designed to be map-centered, intuitive, and accessible to users without advanced GIS or technical training, emphasizing readability, clear map legends, consistent labels, and straightforward navigation.

Module 1 — Home and System Information Module. This module serves as the entry point of the platform. It presents an overview of AgriKA-GIS, including its purpose, key features, and general information about the system. Users can navigate to other modules from this page and view summary information about the participating cities and the system's capabilities.

Module 2 — Real-Time and Historical Yield Monitoring Module. This module allows users to view both the most recent satellite-derived yield predictions and historical production records. It enables City Agriculturists and Rice Technicians to observe changes in rice productivity over time through continuously updated prediction outputs and time-series comparisons across cropping seasons.

Module 3 — Spatial GIS Visualization and Analysis Module. This is the core spatial module of the platform. It displays predicted rice yield through interactive barangay-level heatmaps and presents residual maps that identify areas where the model over-predicts or under-predicts yield relative to recorded data. Users can apply filters by city, barangay, year, and cropping season to examine specific localities and time periods.

Module 4 — Rice Yield Analytics and Comparison Module. This module provides analytical tools for comparing rice productivity across barangays, cities, and cropping seasons. Module 5 — Reports Generation and Data Import/Export Module. This module enables authorized users to generate and download rice yield reports in PDF, Excel, and CSV formats. It also supports importing agricultural records, allowing the system to be updated as new production data becomes available from the City Agriculture Offices.

Module 6 — User Access Management and System Configuration Module. This module manages user accounts, authentication, and role-based access control. Administrators can create and manage accounts, maintain system records, and configure platform settings.

Security Design

AgriKA-GIS will include role-based access control to protect agricultural information and restrict system functions according to user responsibilities. The provincial-level Administrator has the broadest access, managing users, system configuration, and province-wide records, while Agriculturists and Rice Technicians access only the information for their assigned city or municipality. This design supports secure, jurisdiction-specific access while preventing unauthorized modification or viewing of restricted information.

CHAPTER 4

Results and Discussion

This chapter presents the results obtained during the development and evaluation of AgriKA-GIS. The discussion is organized according to the specific objectives of the study. The first section describes how the Agile Software Development Life Cycle was applied during system development. The succeeding sections present the results for Objective 1, covering the construction of the dataset and the development and evaluation of the extended CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model; Objective 2, covering the development, testing, and user evaluation of the Web-based spatial decision-support system; and Objective 3, covering the implementation and reliability evaluation of the automated data pipeline.

Agile Development Implementation

The development of AgriKA-GIS followed the Agile Software Development Life Cycle described in the methodology. Rather than completing each phase once in sequence, the researchers carried out development in short iterations, with each iteration passing through planning, design, development, testing, and refinement before the next iteration began. All source code was maintained in a Git version control repository, which served as the documentary record of what was built in each iteration and when refinements were introduced.

Each iteration was followed by a review period during which the working build was examined against the requirements identified in the Requirements Gathering phase and, where applicable, discussed with the thesis adviser. The findings from each review determined the scope of the succeeding iteration. Table 8 summarizes the five iterations, the Agile phases exercised in each, and the outcomes that were carried forward.

Table 8

Summary of Agile Development Iterations

IterationDurationAgile Phases ExercisedFocus and DeliverablesOutcome Carried Forward
1July 4-10, 2026System Planning and Design; DevelopmentProject repository initialization; React and Vite frontend scaffolding; translation of the approved interface designs into the Home, Portal Access, and Reports and Data Import/Export componentsInterface shell completed, but all displayed values were static; a persistent data layer was required
2August 6-9, 2026Development; Testing and Refinement; DeploymentFlask backend with JWT authentication and role-based authorization; PostgreSQL and PostGIS schema; import of Laguna administrative boundaries; compilation of historical municipality yield records; connection of the Monitoring, Spatial GIS, Analytics, and Reports modules to live data; deployment to a cloud environmentFour of six modules operating on real data; prediction overlay left as an empty scaffold pending model output

5September 2026Requirements Gathering; Development; Testing and Refinement; DeploymentAutomated acquisition of Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and meteorological data; feature tables added to the spatial database; single-command pipeline orchestrator; recreation and training of the CNN-LSTM model; feature ablation and paired significance testing; export of model predictions into the spatial database and activation of the predicted-yield and residual viewsPrediction and residual components operating on real model output; barangay-level prediction outstanding

Iteration 1 established the project structure and translated the approved interface designs into working frontend components. At the close of this iteration the interface was navigable but displayed only static placeholder values, since no backend or database had yet been implemented. The review of this build confirmed that a persistent data layer was the prerequisite for every remaining module.

Iteration 2 was the largest of the interface-development iterations. The researchers implemented the Flask backend, established the PostgreSQL and PostGIS database according to the database design, imported the Laguna administrative boundaries as spatial geometry, and compiled the historical municipality-level yield records into the database. Four of the six modules were then connected to live data. Role-based authorization was implemented through JSON Web Tokens carrying the authenticated user's role and assigned municipality as claims, so that requests for data outside a user's jurisdiction were rejected at the application layer rather than filtered at the interface. The system was deployed to a cloud environment at the end of this iteration to allow the build to be reviewed outside the researchers' development machines.

Iteration 3 responded to observations gathered during the review of the deployed build. Because the deployment used a service tier that suspends idle applications, the first request after a period of inactivity was delayed while the backend resumed. This produced an ambiguous blank state that reviewers could not distinguish from a system failure. The researchers therefore added an explicit backend availability indicator to the login page and an overlay describing the resumption process. Map tiles that painted after the loading overlay had already been dismissed were also corrected in this iteration. These refinements did not add functionality but addressed interpretability problems that would have affected user evaluation.

Iteration 4 addressed the spatial drill-down interaction, which is central to Objective 2. The researchers implemented municipality-to-barangay drill-in on the interactive map, with a localized loading state confined to the map region, and completed the barangay-level choropleth rendering. Because barangay-level yield values were not yet available, the choropleth was verified using generated sample values derived from each municipality's recorded yield. These values are returned by the system with an explicit flag identifying them as sample data and are labeled as such in the interface. They were used solely to confirm that the boundary retrieval, value binding, color classification, and legend components of the rendering pipeline operated correctly across all barangays of a municipality, and they are not presented anywhere in this study as prediction or observation results.

Iteration 5 completed the data and modelling work on which the remaining system functions depended. The automated acquisition, preprocessing, and integration pipeline described under Objective 3 was implemented and executed, the resulting features were loaded into the spatial database, and the prediction model described under Objective 1 was recreated, trained, and evaluated. Model predictions were then exported into the municipality predictions table, which activated the predicted-yield overlay and the residual comparison that had been scaffolded but left unpopulated since Iteration 2. This iteration also produced the feature ablation and the paired significance test reported under Objective 1.

Across the five iterations, the six Agile phases defined in the methodology were exercised as follows. Requirements Gathering was completed prior to Iteration 1 and revisited when review findings indicated unmet needs, most substantially in Iteration 5 when the data requirements of the prediction model were established in detail. System Planning and Design was concentrated in Iteration 1 but returned to in Iteration 2 when the database schema was finalized and again in Iteration 5 when the feature tables were added. Development and Testing and Refinement recurred in every iteration. Deployment first occurred in Iteration 2 and was maintained thereafter, allowing each subsequent build to be reviewed in its deployed state rather than only in development. Review and Feedback occurred between iterations and determined the scope of the succeeding one, which is most clearly demonstrated by Iteration 3, whose entire scope was derived from findings raised during the review of the Iteration 2 build.

Objective 1: Extended CNN-LSTM Rice Yield Prediction Model

This section presents the results of the dataset construction and the development and evaluation of the extended CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model. The dataset is discussed first, followed by the training protocol, the performance of the evaluated models, the paired statistical comparison establishing the contribution of Sentinel-1, the feature ablation, and the comparison against the previous AgriKA model.

Scope of the Model Evaluation

The model was trained and evaluated on all 29 rice-producing municipalities and cities of Laguna rather than on the four participating cities alone. Two considerations determined this. First, the four cities yield only 64 municipality-season observations across the study period, which is insufficient both for training a model of this architecture and for the paired statistical comparison required by the objective. Second, the previous AgriKA model was itself trained province-wide, and a comparison conducted on a different geographic base would not isolate the contribution of Sentinel-1. The four participating cities remain the evaluation site for the decision-support system reported under Objective 2, where the User Acceptance Testing is conducted with their agriculture personnel.

Final Dataset Construction

Municipality-Level Observed Yield Records

Historical average palay yield records for the province of Laguna were compiled from sixteen separate municipality-level exports, one for each year and semester from 2018 to 2025. Each export covers the entire Philippines and identifies its reporting period only in the file name rather than within the data, so the records could not be used directly. A compilation routine was written to read each export, retain only the municipalities of Laguna, tag every row with the year and season parsed from the file name, normalize municipality names so that they match the names already present in the spatial database, and write the combined result in both a long format suitable for loading into the database and a wide municipality-by-period format suitable for inspection.

The compilation produced 462 municipality-season records covering 29 of the 30 municipalities and cities of Laguna. San Pedro was excluded because it has no rice-producing area, which is consistent with the exclusion applied in the previous AgriKA study. Twenty-eight municipalities have the complete set of sixteen records; Rizal has fourteen, as two reporting periods were absent from the source exports. Table 9 summarizes the coverage of the compiled dataset.

The compilation routine also produced a validation report identifying values that appear to have been backfilled in the source dataset. Where several municipalities in the same reporting period share an identical yield value to five decimal places, the value is unlikely to represent an independent measurement for each municipality. Eight such values were detected and flagged.

The flag is carried into the database and is available to the interface so that affected values can be qualified rather than silently presented as independent observations. Table 10 presents sample records for the four participating cities.

Satellite and Meteorological Data Acquisition

Satellite and meteorological data were acquired for the full study period through the automated pipeline described under Objective 3. Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 acquisitions were retrieved from the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem and meteorological variables from the Open-Meteo service, in both cases aggregated to monthly values per municipality. The study period comprises 30 municipalities across eight years and twelve months, giving 2,880 expected area-months. Table 11 presents the acquisition and completeness results.

Table 11

Coverage of the Acquired Satellite and Meteorological Data

Data sourceVariablesArea-months acquiredCompleteness
Open-MeteoRainfall, temperature, relative humidity2,880 of 2,880 (100%)100%
Sentinel-2 (optical)NDVI, EVI, NDWI2,850 of 2,880 (99.0%)89.9% after cloud screening
Sentinel-1 (SAR)VV and VH backscatter2,850 of 2,880 (99.0%)99.0%

Meteorological coverage is complete, as the Open-Meteo service provides continuous reanalysis values that are not subject to observational gaps. Sentinel-1 coverage is effectively complete wherever an acquisition was made, which is the expected behavior of synthetic aperture radar, since microwave backscatter is not obstructed by cloud. Sentinel-2 completeness is lower at 89.9%, and the gaps are not randomly distributed: 183 of the 261 optical gaps fall within the wet season. This concentration is the empirical expression of the limitation that motivated the study. In a tropical setting the optical sensor is least available precisely during the season when monitoring is most consequential, and it is this asymmetry that gives Sentinel-1 its role in the model.

Feature Engineering and Final Dataset

Monthly features were aligned to the two cropping seasons defined by the Philippine Statistics Authority semester convention and assembled into six-timestep sequences per municipality-season, matching the temporal structure the recurrent layers of the model are intended to learn. Merging the feature sequences with the observed yield records produced the final training set. All 29 municipalities carrying yield labels were successfully matched to their features, and 462 training rows were delivered, corresponding exactly to the 462 observed yield records. Table 12 presents the final feature set.

The Enhanced Vegetation Index and the Normalized Difference Water Index were acquired and retained in the training dataset but excluded from both model configurations, for the reasons established by the feature ablation reported later in this section.

Model Development and Training Protocol

The previous AgriKA model (Ebron et al., 2025) was reimplemented in PyTorch as the baseline for comparison. The reimplementation reproduces the architecture reported as their final configuration: two one-dimensional convolutional layers of 64 and 128 filters with a kernel size of five, two stacked LSTM layers of 128 and 64 units, two dense layers of 64 and 32 units, Gaussian noise of 0.01 applied during training, the Adam optimizer at a learning rate of 4.5 × 10⁻⁴, and L2 regularization of 1 × 10⁻⁴.

Two adaptations were necessary and are documented here for transparency. Pooling was omitted, because the input sequences in this study consist of six timesteps and pooling would have collapsed the temporal axis the LSTM layers are intended to model. Recurrent dropout was approximated rather than applied directly, as the CUDA-accelerated LSTM implementation in PyTorch does not support it. Neither adaptation differs between the two configurations compared below, so neither affects the measured contribution of Sentinel-1.

The evaluation followed a leave-one-year-out cross-validation protocol across the eight years from 2018 to 2025. In each fold the model was trained on seven years and evaluated on the withheld year, and the out-of-fold predictions were pooled to produce a single set of 462 predictions in which every observation was predicted by a model that had not seen its year during training. This protocol was chosen over a random split because rice yield is temporally autocorrelated; a random split would allow the model to interpolate within a year it had partly memorized, inflating performance.

Two configurations of the same architecture were trained. The baseline configuration used rainfall, temperature, humidity, and Sentinel-2 NDVI, corresponding to the input classes available to the previous AgriKA model. The enhanced configuration added Sentinel-1 VV and VH backscatter. All other elements — architecture, target variable, training protocol, and fold assignment — were held identical, so that the difference between the two runs isolates the contribution of Sentinel-1. Table 13 summarizes the configuration.

Table 13

Model Training Configuration and Held-Constant Parameters

ElementSpecification

RegularizationGaussian noise 0.01; L2 1 × 10⁻⁴
OptimizerAdam, learning rate 4.5 × 10⁻⁴
Target variableObserved municipality seasonal yield (metric tons per hectare)

Model Performance

Table 14 presents the pooled out-of-fold performance of the two configurations, together with a Random Forest regressor trained on the same features and folds. The Random Forest was included not as a competing contribution but as a reference point indicating what a conventional ensemble method achieves on this dataset.

Table 14

Pooled Out-of-Fold Performance of the Evaluated Models

ModelFeaturesRMSEMAER²
Random Forest (reference)Sentinel-2 + Sentinel-10.4860.3870.202
CNN-LSTM, baseline configurationSentinel-2 only0.5260.4210.075
CNN-LSTM, enhanced configurationSentinel-2 + Sentinel-10.5030.3950.152

The enhanced configuration outperformed the baseline on all three metrics. Root mean squared error fell from 0.526 to 0.503 metric tons per hectare, mean absolute error from 0.421 to 0.395, and the coefficient of determination rose from 0.075 to 0.152, approximately doubling the proportion of variance explained. The direction of improvement is consistent across every metric, which is what would be expected if the added inputs carry genuine signal rather than noise that happens to favour one measure.

Figure 18. Observed Versus Predicted Yield for the Baseline and Enhanced Configurations
