Statistical Comparison of the Two Configurations

Because both configurations produced predictions for the same 462 observations, the two error distributions are paired and can be compared directly. For each observation the absolute error of the enhanced configuration was subtracted from the absolute error of the baseline configuration, so that a positive difference indicates that the enhanced configuration was closer to the observed value.

A Shapiro-Wilk test on the paired differences returned W = 0.990 with p = 0.003, rejecting normality at the 0.05 significance level. The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test was therefore adopted as the primary test, following the decision rule stated in the methodology. A paired t-test is reported alongside it for corroboration, since the sample is large enough for the t-test to remain informative under mild departures from normality. Table 15 presents the results.

Table 15

Paired Comparison of Baseline and Enhanced Configuration Errors

StatisticValue
Paired observations462
Mean absolute error, baseline configuration0.4205 mt/ha
Mean absolute error, enhanced configuration0.3950 mt/ha
Mean improvement0.0255 mt/ha (6.1% error reduction)
Observations improved by the enhanced configuration254 of 462 (55.0%)
Shapiro-Wilk test of paired differencesW = 0.990, p = 0.003 (not normal)
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test (primary)W = 47,153, p = 0.028
Paired t-test (corroborating)t = 2.40, p = 0.017
Effect size (Cohen's d, paired)0.11

Both tests reject the null hypothesis of no difference at the 0.05 significance level. The improvement attributable to Sentinel-1 is therefore statistically significant and is unlikely to have arisen by chance.

The magnitude of that improvement should be stated with equal precision. A 6.1% reduction in mean absolute error and a Cohen's d of 0.11 constitute a small effect. The enhanced configuration was closer to the observed value in 55.0% of cases, meaning that in 45.0% of cases the baseline configuration was closer. The finding is that Sentinel-1 makes a consistent and detectable contribution, not that it transforms predictive performance.

Feature Ablation

Three feature sets were evaluated through the identical pipeline in order to determine which of the variables named in the methodology contributed to model performance. Table 16 presents the results.

Table 16

Feature Ablation Results

Feature setEnhanced configuration R²Significance of Sentinel-1 contribution
Rainfall, temperature, NDVI0.085p = 0.003
Plus humidity (final set)0.152p = 0.028
Plus EVI and NDWI0.066p = 0.61

The addition of humidity produced the single largest improvement observed in this study, raising the coefficient of determination of the enhanced configuration from 0.085 to 0.152. This is consistent with the role of relative humidity in the tropical rice-growing environment, where it bears on both evapotranspiration and disease pressure.

The addition of the Enhanced Vegetation Index and the Normalized Difference Water Index degraded performance, reducing R² to 0.066 and eliminating the statistical significance of the Sentinel-1 contribution. Two factors account for this. First, EVI proved numerically unstable on this dataset, producing values as high as approximately 3.0, well outside the range within which the index is normally interpreted. Second, both indices are computed from the same spectral bands as NDVI and are therefore substantially correlated with it. On a dataset of 462 observations, the additional correlated dimensions imposed a greater cost in variance than the information they contributed.

The final feature set is therefore rainfall, temperature, humidity, and NDVI, with Sentinel-1 VV and VH added in the enhanced configuration. EVI and NDWI were retained in the training dataset so that this ablation remains reproducible, but were excluded from the models reported above. This result also indicates that the interaction between feature selection and the measured Sentinel-1 effect is not incidental: the same architecture and the same SAR inputs yielded a significant contribution under two feature sets and no detectable contribution under a third.

Figure 21. Feature Ablation — Effect on Model R².

Model Comparison and Normalized Composite Accuracy Index

The methodology specifies that candidate models be ranked using a Normalized Composite Accuracy Index, in which each evaluation metric is normalized across the candidate set and combined into a single score. The index was computed across the three evaluated models, with root mean squared error and mean absolute error inverted so that a higher normalized score indicates better performance in every case, and the three normalized components weighted equally. Table 17 presents the result.

Table 17

Normalized Composite Accuracy Index Across the Evaluated Models

ModelNormalized RMSENormalized MAENormalized R²NCAIRank
Random Forest (reference)1.0001.0001.0001.0001
CNN-LSTM, enhanced configuration0.5750.7650.6060.6492
CNN-LSTM, baseline configuration0.0000.0000.0000.0003

Because the index normalizes across the candidate set, the best and worst performers necessarily receive scores of one and zero on each component, and with only three candidates the index conveys ranking rather than absolute distance. The ranking is nonetheless unambiguous and consistent with the individual metrics: the enhanced configuration ranks above the baseline configuration on every component, confirming that the selection between the two CNN-LSTM configurations does not depend on which metric is given priority. The enhanced configuration was therefore adopted as the final model of this study.

Comparison with the Previous AgriKA Model

The comparison reported above is an ablation conducted within this study rather than a direct comparison against the published performance of the previous AgriKA model, and the reason should be stated plainly, since it bears on how the result may be interpreted.

Ebron et al. (2025) trained their model on an "Adjusted Yield" target, in which each season's total yield was redistributed across three growth phases using a green-ratio weighting. Their target therefore has a mean of approximately 1.2 metric tons per hectare, whereas the present study predicts observed seasonal yield with a mean of 4.215. Root mean squared error and mean absolute error are expressed in the units of the target and are consequently not comparable across the two studies; an RMSE of 0.65 on a 1.2 mt/ha target represents a substantially larger relative error than an RMSE of 0.50 on a 4.2 mt/ha target. The coefficient of determination, being scale-invariant, is the only one of the three metrics that supports meaningful cross-study comparison. Table 18 presents the comparison on that basis.

Table 18

Comparison with the Previous AgriKA Model

StudyTarget variableTest R²
Ebron et al. (2025)Adjusted Yield (phase-redistributed)0.1649
Present study, baseline configurationObserved seasonal yield0.075
Present study, enhanced configurationObserved seasonal yield0.152

The test coefficient of determination reported by Ebron et al. is used here. Their study also reports a validation R² of 0.3125; comparing that figure against a test result from the present study would compare performance on data used for model selection against performance on withheld data, and would not be a valid comparison.

On this basis the enhanced configuration of the present study performs comparably to the previous AgriKA model, at 0.152 against 0.1649, while predicting a target that was not redistributed and while being evaluated under leave-one-year-out cross-validation rather than a single chronological split. The contribution of this objective is therefore not that the enhanced model surpasses the previous one in absolute accuracy, but that the addition of Sentinel-1 produces a measurable and statistically significant improvement over an equivalent Sentinel-2-only model evaluated under identical conditions — a comparison the previous study could not make, as it did not use SAR data.

Discussion of Model Performance

Three characteristics of these results warrant direct comment.

The Random Forest reference model outperformed both CNN-LSTM configurations, reaching an R² of 0.202 against 0.152 for the enhanced deep model. Deep architectures of the kind used here are designed to learn representations from large datasets, and 462 observations is small by that standard. The result indicates that on a dataset of this size the additional capacity of the convolutional-recurrent architecture was not repaid, and it is reported rather than omitted because it bears on how the modelling approach should be assessed.

The absolute performance of all three models is modest. Observed yields in the dataset cluster within a narrow band, with a mean of 4.215 metric tons per hectare and a standard deviation of approximately 0.55. Because the coefficient of determination expresses the proportion of variance explained, a target with little variance to begin with will produce low values under any method. The enhanced configuration's RMSE of 0.503 sits just below that standard deviation, indicating that the model performs somewhat better than predicting the provincial mean for every observation, but not dramatically so.

Finally, the concentration of Sentinel-2 gaps in the wet season, reported in Table 11, is consistent with the mechanism by which Sentinel-1 is expected to contribute. Whether the SAR contribution is in fact larger during the wet season than the dry season was not tested in this study and is identified in the Recommendations as a question for subsequent work.

Objective 2: Web-Based Spatial Decision-Support System

This section presents the results of the development, testing, and evaluation of the AgriKA-GIS Web-based spatial decision-support system. The system was implemented as a three-tier application consisting of a React and Vite presentation layer, a Flask application layer, and a PostgreSQL and PostGIS data layer, following the architecture presented in the methodology. The results are presented in the order of the six major system modules, followed by the database implementation, the role-based access implementation, the deployment configuration, and the testing and evaluation results.

System Development Results

All six modules defined in the methodology were implemented and operate on live data retrieved from the spatial database, including the predicted-yield and residual views, which were populated once the model output described under Objective 1 was exported into the database. The single exception is barangay-level yield values, which remain generated sample data pending the barangay-level prediction work described under Objective 1, and which are identified as such wherever they appear.

Module 1: Home and System Information

The Home and System Information module was implemented as a set of publicly accessible pages requiring no authentication. It consists of a landing page presenting the purpose and main features of AgriKA-GIS, an About page describing the research team and the participating Local Government Units, a Frequently Asked Questions page, and a Contact page. The landing page also presents the alignment of the system with the Sustainable Development Goals identified in the Rationale of the Study, and includes an introductory walkthrough of the platform. Navigation from these pages leads either to the read-only public yield map or to the Portal Access page, where authorized users authenticate. This module serves as the entry point described in the methodology and orients users who are not part of the LGU workflow.

Figure 20. Home and System Information Interface

Module 2: Real-Time and Historical Yield Monitoring

The Real-Time and Historical Yield Monitoring module presents observed rice yield for a selected year and cropping season alongside an interactive map of the study area. The module retrieves its data from the municipality yield records stored in the spatial database and provides filters for municipality, year, and season. The available years and seasons are derived from the database at runtime rather than hard-coded, so that the filter options always reflect the data actually present. The module presents a ranked list of municipalities by yield, a distribution of municipalities across yield ranges, and a year-over-year trend series for the selected season, computed either for a single municipality or as a provincial average.

Figure 21. Real-Time and Historical Yield Monitoring Interface

Module 3: Spatial GIS Visualization and Analysis

The Spatial GIS Visualization and Analysis module is the core spatial component of the system and was implemented using Leaflet through the react-leaflet library. The module renders the administrative boundaries of Laguna retrieved from the PostGIS database as GeoJSON and shades each municipality according to its observed yield for the selected year and season, producing the municipality-level choropleth. Selecting a municipality drills the map into that municipality and renders its constituent barangay boundaries, with the map view fitted to the selected extent and a localized loading indicator shown while the barangay geometry is retrieved.

The module provides a search function that resolves both municipality and barangay names and drills the map to the matched feature, a layer panel controlling boundary display, and a toggle between a cartographic base map and satellite imagery. Two additional layers, land use and land parcel, were included in the interface in a disabled state with an explicit label indicating the data they require, as neither dataset had been obtained at the time of writing.

The module presents predicted yield as a selectable overlay alongside the observed layer. The system determines the availability of the overlay by querying the municipality predictions table, so that the view activates automatically when model output is present and remains disabled when it is not; following the export of the predictions reported under Objective 1, the overlay operates on real model output. The residual view renders the difference between observed and predicted yield for each municipality, allowing the spatial distribution of prediction error to be examined directly on the map rather than only in tabular form.

Barangay-level shading is presently derived from generated sample values, as described in the Agile Development Implementation section. These values are returned with an explicit flag identifying them as sample data and are labeled as such in the interface. They confirm that boundary retrieval, value binding, color classification, and legend rendering operate correctly across all barangays of a municipality, and they are not reported anywhere in this study as observed or predicted yield. They will be replaced by the barangay-level predictions described under Objective 1.

Figure 22. Spatial GIS Visualization and Analysis Interface

Figure 23. Barangay-Level Drill-In View

Figure 24. Predicted Yield and Residual Overlays

Module 4: Rice Yield Analytics and Comparison

The Rice Yield Analytics and Comparison module provides tabular and graphical comparison of rice yield across municipalities and cropping seasons. Users may compare municipalities against one another for a selected season, or examine a single municipality against the provincial average across years. The module was implemented using the Recharts library and draws on the same municipality yield records used by Module 2, together with a dedicated comparison endpoint that returns observed yield, predicted yield, and the residual for each municipality in a selected year and season.

The comparison endpoint computes the residual as the difference between observed and predicted yield and reports the mean absolute error across all municipalities for which both values exist. With the model output loaded, the module presents the observed and predicted series together with the per-municipality residual, giving users the same error information reported statistically under Objective 1 in a form aligned to their own jurisdiction. The barangay-level comparison view displays an explicit message indicating that barangay-level yield data is not yet available.

Figure 25. Rice Yield Analytics and Comparison Interface

Module 5: Reports Generation and Data Import/Export

The Reports Generation and Data Import/Export module allows authorized users to generate rice yield reports filtered by municipality, year, season, and reporting period, and to group the resulting records for presentation. The module retrieves the complete set of observed municipality yield records from the database and presents a report preview before export. Reports may be exported as CSV, as a spreadsheet-compatible file, or rendered for printing to PDF. A downloadable import template is provided so that records submitted by City Agriculture Offices follow the expected column structure.

The import function accepts a CSV file through a drag-and-drop area, parses it, validates its structure, and appends the parsed records to the working report set, recording the file name, row count, and import time in an import log. The parser was implemented as an explicit state machine rather than a pattern-matching expression so that malformed or adversarial input cannot cause excessive processing time. At the time of writing, imported records are held within the active session and are not yet written to the spatial database; server-side persistence of imported yield records is identified in the Recommendations as remaining work.

Figure 26. Reports Generation and Data Import/Export Interface

Module 6: User Access Management and System Configuration

The User Access Management and System Configuration module was implemented as an administrator-only interface for managing portal accounts. Administrators may create accounts, assign a role and a municipality, edit account details, change account status, and remove accounts. The role and municipality options presented in the interface are retrieved from the database rather than defined in the interface, so that they remain consistent with the underlying records. Accounts are created by the Administrator; the system provides no self-service registration, which preserves the administrator-provisioned access model described in the Security Design.

Passwords are never stored in plain text. Each password is hashed before storage, and the authentication endpoint returns an identical error message for an unknown username and for an incorrect password, so that the response does not reveal which of the two was wrong.

Figure 27. User Access Management and System Configuration Interface

Database Implementation

The database was implemented in PostgreSQL with the PostGIS extension, following the entity relationship diagram presented in the methodology. Twelve tables were created: roles, municipalities, users, barangays, seasons, predictions, yield_records, municipality_yield_records, municipality_predictions, residuals, weather_monthly, and satellite_monthly. Indexes were created on the foreign keys used most frequently in query filtering, specifically the municipality, barangay, and season references.

The administrative boundaries of Laguna were prepared in QGIS and imported into the database as PostGIS geometry, comprising the provincial boundary, 30 municipalities and cities, and 682 barangays. Barangay boundary geometry is stored in a dedicated geometry column added after the PostGIS extension is enabled, allowing the non-spatial portion of the system, including authentication and user management, to operate independently of the spatial extension during setup.

Two pairs of tables store yield information. The barangay-keyed predictions and yield_records tables correspond to the barangay-level granularity that is the central contribution of the study. The municipality-keyed municipality_yield_records and municipality_predictions tables store the historical records and model output presently available at municipality level. Keeping these separate rather than aggregating them into a single table preserves the distinction between the two granularities and prevents municipality-level values from being reported as though they were barangay-level observations. Observed municipality yield records carry a source field naming their origin and a proxy flag marking the eight values discussed under Objective 1. Predicted values carry a model version and a generation timestamp, allowing the output of several model runs to coexist and the most recent run to be selected automatically.

The weather_monthly and satellite_monthly tables hold the acquired meteorological and satellite features, described under Objective 3. Their inclusion in the same database as the boundaries, yield records, and predictions constitutes the centralized spatial database specified by the methodology, in which every dataset the study acquires or produces is stored in one queryable location rather than distributed across intermediate files.

Figure. AgriKA-GIS Database Schema (Entity-Relationship Diagram).

Role-Based Access Implementation

Role-based access control was implemented using JSON Web Tokens. On successful authentication the server issues a token whose identity is the user account identifier and which carries the user's role and assigned municipality as additional claims. The token expires after eight hours. Every protected endpoint verifies the token and evaluates the role claim before performing any query, so that an unauthorized request is rejected at the application layer rather than merely hidden from the interface. Administrator-only endpoints return an explicit authorization error when the role claim is not that of an administrator.

The interface enforces the same rules a second time. Each protected route is wrapped in a guard that compares the authenticated user's role against the roles permitted for that route, and the navigation sidebar presents only the modules available to the user's role. The Administrator operates province-wide and is not scoped to a single municipality, while Agriculturists and Rice Technicians are scoped to their assigned city. System Deployment

The system was deployed to a cloud environment so that it could be reviewed and evaluated without requiring local installation. The Flask application was deployed as a web service running under a production application server, the React frontend was built and deployed as a static site, and the PostgreSQL and PostGIS database was hosted on a managed database service. Cross-origin requests are restricted to the deployed frontend origin, and the token signing key and database connection string are supplied as environment variables rather than stored in the source repository.

Because the deployment uses a service tier that suspends the application after a period of inactivity, the first request following an idle period is delayed while the service resumes. The login page therefore queries the health endpoint and displays the current availability of the backend, and an overlay explains the delay to the user. This behavior is a property of the hosting tier rather than of the system itself and is noted here because it affects how evaluation sessions should be conducted.

Objective 3: Secure Automated Data Pipeline

This section presents the results of the implementation and evaluation of the data pipeline that acquires, processes, integrates, and manages the datasets required by the prediction model and the spatial decision-support system. The pipeline was implemented in full and evaluated on its reliability across the five stages named in the objective.

Pipeline Architecture and Implementation

The pipeline was implemented as a set of stage-specific routines coordinated by a single orchestrator. Table 26 presents the stages, their implementation, and their outputs.

Table 26

Data Pipeline Stages and Implementation

StageImplementationOutput
AcquisitionAutomated retrieval of meteorological variables from Open-Meteo and Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 acquisitions from the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem, with resume capability so that an interrupted run continues from the last completed request rather than restartingRaw monthly observations per municipality
PreprocessingCloud and scene-classification masking of optical imagery, conversion of SAR backscatter to decibels, reprojection to the appropriate UTM zone, monthly aggregation, guards against non-finite values, and explicit gap handlingCleaned monthly feature values
IntegrationMerging of meteorological and satellite features and alignment to the Philippine Statistics Authority semester convention defining the cropping seasonsMunicipality-season feature sequences
StorageLoading into the weather_monthly and satellite_monthly PostGIS tables through an idempotent upsert keyed on municipality, year, and month, with diacritics-folded name matching against the municipality recordsFeatures stored in the centralized spatial database
DeliveryExport of the training feature set in wide and sequence formats for the model, and export of model predictions into the municipality_predictions table for the decision-support systemTraining data and predictions available to downstream components

The uniqueness constraint on municipality, year, and month, combined with upsert semantics, makes every stage re-runnable without duplicating records. A stage that is executed twice produces the same database state as a stage executed once, which is the property that allows the pipeline to be re-run after a partial failure without manual cleanup.

Credentials for the external services are supplied through environment variables loaded from a file excluded from version control. No credential appears in the source code or in the repository history, which satisfies the security requirement stated in the objective.

Figure 31. Data Pipeline Architecture

Figure 31. Data Pipeline Architecture.

Pipeline Orchestration

The five stages were placed under a single orchestrator that executes them in dependency order: acquire meteorological data, acquire satellite data, ensure the database tables exist, load the features into the database, and build the training set. Each stage reports its status and elapsed time, and by default the run halts at the first failure so that a downstream stage never executes on incomplete input. An option to continue past failures is provided for diagnostic runs, and an option to skip the acquisition stages allows the integration and loading stages to be re-executed without issuing further requests to the external services, which matters because the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem imposes a processing-unit quota.

Each run writes a machine-readable summary recording which stages executed, their outcomes, and their durations. This summary is the record against which the reliability evaluation reported below is conducted, and it constitutes the evidence that the pipeline operates without manual intervention between stages.

Reliability Evaluation

The pipeline was evaluated against the criteria stated in the objective: reliable acquisition, correct preprocessing, accurate integration, and consistent delivery. The evaluation was conducted by a routine that queries the spatial database and the delivered training set directly, rather than by inspecting intermediate files, so that the result reflects the state of the data as the downstream components receive it. The evaluation scope is 30 municipalities across eight years and twelve months, or 2,880 expected area-months. Table 27 presents the results.

Table 27

Pipeline Reliability Evaluation Results

CriterionMeasureResult
AcquisitionArea-months retrieved against expectedMeteorological 2,880 of 2,880 (100%); satellite 2,850 of 2,880 (99.0%); all 30 municipalities represented
CompletenessProportion of retrieved area-months carrying usable valuesMeteorological features 100%; optical indices 89.9%; SAR backscatter 99.0%
IntegrityValues outside physical range or non-finite0 violations; 4 EVI outliers noted and the index excluded from the final model
IntegrationYield-label municipalities successfully matched to features29 of 29 (100%); 462 training rows delivered
Gap accountingDistribution and magnitude of missing area-months183 of 261 optical gaps fall in the wet season; SAR complete wherever acquired; 1.0% of area-months absent across all sources

The pipeline recorded no integrity violations. Every value delivered to the model lies within the physical range of its variable and none is non-finite, which means that the guards applied during preprocessing operated as intended across the full study period rather than only on the cases encountered during development. Integration is likewise complete: all 29 municipalities carrying yield labels were matched to their features despite the differences in naming and diacritics between the yield exports, the boundary data, and the database records, and the delivered training set contains exactly the 462 rows expected from the yield records.

The one incomplete criterion is optical completeness at 89.9%, and the gap accounting establishes that this is a property of the observing conditions rather than of the pipeline. Of the 261 optical gaps, 183 fall within the wet season, when cloud cover over Laguna is persistent. A pipeline cannot retrieve an unclouded optical observation that was never made. What the pipeline can do, and does, is record the gap explicitly rather than silently interpolating over it, so that the absence is visible to the model and to this evaluation. The corresponding SAR coverage is complete wherever an acquisition was made, which is the behavior that motivated the inclusion of Sentinel-1 in the study.

Deviation from the Stated Methodology

One documented deviation should be recorded. The methodology names the Green Ratio, computed as the ratio of the near-infrared to the green band, among the Sentinel-2 indices to be acquired. The pipeline as implemented computes the Normalized Difference Water Index in its place. This index was retained in the acquired dataset but, as reported under Objective 1, was found to degrade model performance and was excluded from the final feature set. The Green Ratio was not acquired and its contribution was therefore not tested. Given that the two other indices computed from the same bands were found to be redundant with NDVI on this dataset, a substantial contribution from the Green Ratio appears unlikely, but this remains an untested expectation rather than a finding.

CHAPTER 5

Conclusion and Recommendations

Conclusion

This study set out to determine whether extending the existing AgriKA CNN-LSTM rice yield prediction model through the integration of Sentinel-1 SAR-derived information, barangay-level spatial analysis, and a Web-GIS platform improves rice yield prediction performance and spatial decision support for Local Government Unit agriculture offices in Laguna. The conclusions are presented per specific objective.

Objective 1

The study developed an extended CNN-LSTM model integrating Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter with Sentinel-2 NDVI, meteorological variables, and historical yield records, and evaluated it under leave-one-year-out cross-validation across the eight years from 2018 to 2025. The enhanced model achieved a root mean squared error of 0.503 metric tons per hectare, a mean absolute error of 0.395, and a coefficient of determination of 0.152.

The addition of Sentinel-1 produced a statistically significant improvement over an equivalent Sentinel-2-only model evaluated on identical observations. Mean absolute error fell from 0.421 to 0.395 metric tons per hectare, a reduction of 6.1%, significant under the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test at p = 0.028 and corroborated by a paired t-test at p = 0.017. The effect is small, with a Cohen's d of 0.11, and the study concludes that Sentinel-1 makes a consistent and measurable contribution to rice yield prediction in this setting rather than a transformative one.

Two further findings qualify this conclusion. Relative humidity contributed more to model performance than Sentinel-1 did, nearly doubling the coefficient of determination when added. And a Random Forest regressor trained on the same data outperformed the deep architecture, indicating that on a dataset of 462 observations the capacity of a convolutional-recurrent model is not repaid. The study concludes that the value of the present approach lies in the demonstrated contribution of SAR data rather than in the superiority of the architecture.

State the number of rice-producing barangays covered, the agreement between area-weighted aggregated barangay predictions and the observed municipal values, and the limitation that barangay predictions are validated by aggregation consistency rather than against observed barangay yields.]

Objective 2

The study developed a Web-based spatial decision-support system for rice productivity monitoring in Laguna. All six modules specified in the methodology were implemented as a three-tier application, with the spatial visualization module rendering the administrative boundaries of the province from a PostGIS spatial database and supporting drill-in from municipality to barangay across all 682 barangays of Laguna. Predicted yield and residual views operate on the output of the model developed under Objective 1, allowing prediction error to be examined spatially rather than only in aggregate. Role-based access control was implemented and enforced both at the application layer and in the interface, restricting Agriculturists and Rice Technicians to their assigned city while granting the Administrator province-wide oversight, consistent with the reporting hierarchy of the participating offices. The system was deployed to a cloud environment and is reachable without local installation.

Objective 3

The study implemented and evaluated a secure automated data pipeline covering acquisition, preprocessing, integration, storage, and delivery of Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, meteorological, and historical yield data into a centralized spatial database. The pipeline executes as a single orchestrated sequence with stage-level status reporting and stop-on-failure behavior, and every stage is idempotent, allowing a run to be repeated after a partial failure without duplicating records or requiring manual cleanup. Credentials are supplied through environment variables and appear nowhere in the source repository.

The reliability evaluation recorded complete meteorological acquisition, satellite acquisition at 99.0% of expected area-months, zero integrity violations across all delivered values, and complete integration of all 29 yield-label municipalities with their features, delivering the full set of 462 training rows. Optical completeness of 89.9% reflects cloud cover rather than pipeline failure, with 183 of 261 gaps concentrated in the wet season; these gaps are recorded explicitly rather than interpolated over. The study concludes that the pipeline reliably acquires, preprocesses, integrates, and delivers the data required by the prediction model and the decision-support system, and that its gap accounting provides empirical support for the premise on which the inclusion of Sentinel-1 rests.

Recommendations

Based on the results and the limitations encountered during development, the following recommendations are offered.

Acquisition of rice-producing barangay records. Barangay-level prediction requires knowing which barangays produce rice and how much area each plants. Priority should be given to obtaining, from the City Agriculture Offices of Biñan, Cabuyao, Calamba, and Santa Rosa, a list of rice-producing barangays with planted or harvested area per season. Area records of this kind are routinely maintained for reporting to the Philippine Statistics Authority and are more likely to be available than barangay-level yield. They serve three purposes simultaneously: identifying which of the 114 barangays in the four cities should receive predictions, supplying the weights for aggregation validation, and allowing the coverage of the study to be stated precisely.

Server-side persistence of imported records. The data import function currently parses and validates submitted records within the active session but does not write them to the spatial database. Implementing a write endpoint, with validation and authorization consistent with the existing user management endpoints, would allow Rice Technicians to encode and submit barangay yield records directly into the system as described in the User Profile, and would establish a continuing source of ground-truth data after the study concludes.

Scheduling of the acquisition pipeline. The pipeline executes reliably on demand but is presently invoked manually. Placing it on a schedule aligned to the cropping calendar, so that newly available imagery and meteorological data are ingested and processed without intervention, would complete the automation criterion and would keep the decision-support system current between reporting periods.

Hosting arrangements for evaluation and deployment. The hosting tier used during development suspends the application after a period of inactivity, delaying the first request. For User Acceptance Testing sessions and for any operational use by LGU offices, a tier without suspension should be used, so that evaluators assess the system rather than the characteristics of the hosting plan.

Future research. The concentration of Sentinel-2 gaps in the wet season, established in this study's reliability evaluation, suggests that the contribution of Sentinel-1 may be seasonally uneven. Subsequent studies should test directly whether the SAR contribution is larger during the wet season, when optical imagery is least available, than during the dry season; the present study established that the contribution exists but did not decompose it by season. Studies may also examine whether barangay-level prediction outputs measurably change the intervention decisions made by LGU agriculture offices, which would test the practical premise on which this study is built.
